The Chapter of al-Muddaththir (The Cloaked One) is Meccan, according to all scholars. It has fifty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn, and glorify your Lord, and purify your garments.﴾

There are six issues in this verse.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, meaning, O you who has wrapped himself in his garments, that is, covered himself with them and slept. Its original form is al-mutadaththir, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* because they are similar (in articulation). Ubayy read "al-mutadaththir" according to the original form. Muqatil said: most of this chapter concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who was one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and who used to narrate, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, while narrating about the interruption of revelation, and he said in his hadith: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky, so I raised my head, and behold, the angel who had come to me at Hira was sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was seized with terror [[ji'tu means: I was alarmed and frightened.]] by him, so I returned and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols﴾ (in another narration: before the prayer was made obligatory, and they are the idols). He said: 'Then the revelation followed in succession.'" Al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

Muslim said: Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to us, he said: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, he said: al-Awza'i narrated to us, he said: I heard Yahya say: I asked Abu Salama: "Which Qur'an was revealed first?" He said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾." I said: "Or 'Read'?" He said: "I asked Jabir ibn Abdullah which Qur'an was revealed first, and he said: '﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾.' I said: 'Or "Read"?' Jabir said: 'I will tell you what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us: He said: "I stayed in seclusion at Hira for a month. When I finished my seclusion, I descended and went into the valley's bottom, and I was called. I looked before me, behind me, to my right and to my left, and saw no one. Then I was called again, and I looked and saw no one. Then I was called again, so I raised my head, and behold, he was on the throne in the air," meaning Jibril ﷺ. "A violent trembling seized me, so I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up and poured water over me. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments.﴾"" (al-Bukhari transmitted it, and in it he said:) "I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up and pour cold water over me.' So they wrapped me up and poured cold water over me, and this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols. And do not give to receive more.﴾"

Ibn al-Arabi said: Some exegetes have said that something happened to the Prophet ﷺ from Uqba [ibn Rabi'a [[The addition is from Ibn al-Arabi.]]], so he returned to his home grieved, became agitated and lay down, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. This is false.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: It was said that the statement of the disbelievers of Mecca, "You are a sorcerer," reached him, and he felt grief from that and became feverish, so he wrapped himself in his garments. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, do not dwell on their words, and convey the message to them. It was also said: Abu Lahab, Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-As ibn Wa'il and Mut'im ibn Adi gathered and said: "The delegations of the Arabs have gathered during the days of the Hajj, and they ask one another about the matter of Muhammad, and you have disagreed in reporting about him. One says he is mad, another says he is a soothsayer, another says he is a poet, and the Arabs know that all of this does not combine in one man. So name Muhammad with one name on which they can agree, and the Arabs will call him by it." A man among them stood and said: "A poet." Al-Walid said: "I have heard the speech of Ibn al-Abras and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and the speech of Muhammad does not resemble the speech of either of them." They said: "A soothsayer." He said: "A soothsayer speaks truth and lies, and Muhammad has never lied at all." Another stood and said: "A madman." Al-Walid said: "The madman chokes people, and Muhammad has never choked anyone at all." Al-Walid returned to his house, and they said: "al-Walid ibn al-Mughira has turned away." Abu Jahl entered upon him and said: "What is wrong with you, O Abu Abd Shams? These are the Quraysh gathering something for you, which they will give you. They claim that you are in need and have turned away." Al-Walid said: "I have no need for that, but I thought about Muhammad, and I said: What is the sorcerer's work?" It was said: "He separates the father from his son, the brother from his brother, and the woman from her husband." I said: "He is a sorcerer." This spread among the people, and they began to shout: "Muhammad is a sorcerer." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to his house grieved, and he wrapped himself in a qatifa (a thick cloak), and ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed.

Ikrima said: The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: the one wrapped in prophethood and its burdens. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a distant metaphor, because he had not yet been made a prophet. And also, since this was the first of the Qur'an, he had not yet become accustomed to it, after it had been the second thing revealed.

**Second:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is a gentle address from the Generous to the Beloved, since He called him by his state and described him by his attribute, and did not say "O Muhammad" or "O so-and-so," so that he would feel softness and gentleness from his Lord, as has been mentioned previously in the chapter of al-Muzzammil. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Ali when he slept in the mosque: "Arise, O Abu Turab (father of dust)." He had gone out angry at Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, so his cloak fell off and dust touched him. Muslim transmitted it. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to Hudhayfa on the night of the Trench: "Arise, O sleeper," and this has been mentioned before.

**Third:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, frighten the people of Mecca and warn them of punishment if they do not submit. It was said: warning here means informing them of his prophethood, because it is the prelude to the message. It was said: it is calling them to monotheism, because that is its purpose. Al-Farra' said: Arise and pray, and command others to pray.

**Fourth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, your master, your owner, and the one who sets your affairs right, so magnify Him, and describe Him as greater than having a consort or a son. It is reported in a hadith that they said: "With what should we begin the prayer?" So this was revealed: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, describe Him as greatest. Ibn al-Arabi said: Although this statement, by its generality, requires the takbir of prayer, what is meant by it is the takbir [[As in Ahkam al-Quran, the Cairo edition of Ibn al-Arabi's commentary, 1331 AH. In what the author quoted from Ibn al-Arabi here there is alteration of wording with addition and omission; it should be consulted, vol. 2, p. 287.]], and the sanctification and transcendence, by rejecting rivals and idols besides Him, not taking any protector other than Him, not worshipping anything other than Him, not seeing any act for anyone other than Him, and no blessing except from Him.

It has been narrated that Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalted is Hubal!" and the Prophet ﷺ said: [Say: Allah is higher and more majestic]. This expression has become, by the usage of the Shari'a, the takbir of all acts of worship, adhan, prayer and remembrance, with the words "Allahu Akbar." The words of the Prophet ﷺ that came in an absolute form were interpreted in that sense in several contexts, among them his saying: [Its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam]. The Shari'a in its usage requires what its generality requires. Among its contexts are the times of uttering the name over slaughtered animals for Allah, to single Him out from polytheism, to proclaim His name in sacrifice, and to single out what He has legislated for His command to shed blood.

I say: It has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 175.]] that this expression, "Allahu Akbar," is the one by which worship is performed in prayer, transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. In the exegesis: when Allah's saying, exalted is He, ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood and said: [Allahu Akbar]. Then Khadija said the takbir, and she knew that it was revelation from Allah, exalted is He. Al-Qushayri mentioned it.

**Fifth:** The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾ entered upon the meaning of the answer to a conditional, just as it entered in ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning: arise and warn, and arise and glorify your Lord. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zayd, so strike," meaning: strike Zayd, so the fa' is superfluous.

**Sixth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And purify your garments﴾. In it there are eight opinions. One of them is that what is meant by garments is deeds. The second is the heart. The third is the soul. The fourth is the body. The fifth is the family. The sixth is character. The seventh is religion. The eighth is the garments worn on the outside.

Whoever holds the first opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your deeds," as Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. Mansur narrated from Abu Razin, who said: It means "and your deeds, purify them." He said: When a man has bad deeds, they say "So-and-so has dirty garments," and when he has good deeds, they say "So-and-so has clean garments." Similar to this is reported from al-Suddi. From this is the saying of the poet:

O Allah, indeed Amir ibn Jahm,
or he performed Hajj in filthy garments.
[[Filthy garments: soiled with sins. In the editions: "or dham" with the letter dal, which is a corruption. The meaning of the verse: he performed Hajj while soiled with sins. Awdham al-hajj: he made the Hajj obligatory.]]

And from this is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: [A person will be resurrected in the two garments in which he died]. He meant his good deeds and bad deeds. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

Whoever holds the second opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your heart." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Their evidence is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

So take off my garments from your garments,
[[First half of the verse: "And if you were displeased with some disposition of mine."]]
meaning, my heart from your heart. Al-Mawardi said: They have two views on the interpretation of the verse. One: its meaning is "and purify your heart from sin and disobedience," as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. The second: "and purify your heart from treachery," meaning, do not betray, for then you would be someone with dirty garments. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, and he cited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

By the praise of Allah, I have not worn a garment of wickedness,
nor do I veil myself with treachery.

Whoever holds the third opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your soul," meaning from sins. The Arabs use garments as a metaphor for the soul, as said by Ibn Abbas. From this is the saying of Antara:

So I pierced with the long spear his garments,
the noble one is not forbidden from the spear-points.

And Imru' al-Qays said:
So take off my garments from your garments.

And [[The author attributed this verse later once to Ibn Abi Kabsha and once to Imru' al-Qays. In "al-Lisan" and "Sharh al-Qamus" it is attributed to Imru' al-Qays, but we have not found it in his diwan, and Ibn al-Arabi attributed it to Ibn Abi Kabsha. The last half-verse in the manuscripts is: "And their faces at gatherings are radiant."]] said:

The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces at the places of travel are bright,

meaning, the souls of the Banu Awf. Whoever holds the fourth opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your body," meaning from visible sins. Among what came from the Arabs in using garments as a metaphor for the body is the saying of Layla, when she mentioned camels:

They threw at them light garments, so you see
for them no likeness except the startled ostrich.

Its meaning: they rode them and threw them off by their own selves. As for those who held the fifth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your family, purify them from sins through admonition and discipline." The Arabs call the family a garment, a covering and a wrap. God Most High said: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

Al-Mawardi: For them there are two interpretations of the verse. The first: its meaning is "and your women, purify," by choosing chaste believing women. The second: enjoying them in the front passage and not the rear, in a state of purity and not during menstruation. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

As for those who held the sixth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your character, make good." This was said by al-Hasan and al-Qurazi, because a person's disposition encloses his states just as his garments enclose his self. The poet said:

"Yahya is not blamed for bad character,
and Yahya is pure of garments, free."

That is, of good character.

As for those who held the seventh opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your religion, purify." In the two Sahihs, from him (peace be upon him), he said: "I saw people with garments on them, some of which reached the breasts and some of which were below that, and I saw 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with a waist-wrap that he was dragging." They said: "O Messenger of God, how did you interpret that?" He said: "The religion."

Ibn Wahb related from Malik that he said: "I do not like to recite the Qur'an except in prayer and in mosques, not in the street." God Most High said: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾. Malik intends that he referred to garments by religion (by metonymy).

Abdullah ibn Nafi' related from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, from Malik ibn Anas, regarding His words Most High: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾, that means: do not wear them while treacherous. From this is the saying of Abu Kabsha [see note 3, p. 62 of this part]:

"The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces are white at travel, bright."

By the purity of their garments he means their safety from base acts; by the brightness of their faces their freedom from what is forbidden, or their beauty in creation, or both. This was said by Ibn al-Arabi.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: do not wear your garments over a lie, nor oppression, nor treachery, nor sin. This was said by Ikrima. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Or he blames, in garments, filthy ones."

That is, he has soiled them with sins.

Al-Nabigha said:

"Thin of sandals, fragrant are their waistwraps,
they are greeted with basil on the day of al-Sabasib."

[The verse is from a qasida in praise of Amr ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani. By "thin of sandals" he meant they are kings who do not patch their sandals, and by "fragrant of waistwraps" their chastity. Al-Sabasib is the day of Palm Sunday (al-Sha'anin), a feast day for the Christians, and the one praised was a Christian.]

As for those who held the eighth opinion, they said: the intended meaning is the garments worn. They have four interpretations of it. The first: its meaning is "and your garments, cleanse." From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Garments of the Banu Awf, pure and clean."

The second: "and your garments, lift up and shorten," for shortening garments is further from impurity; when they trail on the ground there is no assurance that something will reach them that makes them impure. This was said by al-Zajjaj and Tawus. The third: "and your garments, purify from impurity with water." This was said by Muhammad ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and the jurists. The fourth: do not wear your garments except from lawful earnings, so that they are purified from the unlawful. It is related from Ibn Abbas: let not your garments that you wear be from an impure source of gain.

Ibn al-Arabi, having mentioned some of what we have mentioned, said: It is not impossible that the verse be taken in its general sense, both literal and figurative. If we take it to mean the known, clean garments, then it comprises two meanings. The first: shortening the hems, for if they are let loose they become soiled. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) said to a young man of the Ansar, when he saw his hem hanging loose: "Raise your waist-wrap, for it is more pious, cleaner and more lasting."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The waist-wrap of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no fault in what lies between that and the ankles, and whatever is below that is in the Fire." So the Prophet (ﷺ) made the limit of the waist-wrap at the ankles and threatened what is beneath it with the Fire. What is the matter with men who let their hems trail, lengthen their garments, and then labour to lift them with their hands? This is the state of pride and the cause of vanity. And the worst of the matter is that they disobey, become impure, and attach themselves to one with whom God has not associated anyone else nor joined anything else to Him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God does not look at the one who drags his garment in arrogance." The wording in the Sahih is: "Whoever drags his waist-wrap in arrogance, God will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, one side of my waist-wrap slips down unless I take care of it?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You are not among those who do it out of arrogance." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the prohibition general and excepted al-Siddiq. The lowly then wished to attach themselves to the exalted, but that is not for them.

The second meaning: washing them from impurity, which is evident from it and sound in it. Al-Mahdawi said: With it some scholars have argued for the obligation of the purity of the garment. Ibn Sirin and Ibn Zayd said: do not pray except in a pure garment. Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence for the obligation of the garment's purity, whereas according to Malik and the people of Madina it is not an obligation, and likewise the purity of the body. What indicates this is the consensus on the permissibility of prayer after cleaning with stones without washing. This matter has been discussed fully in Surat al-Bara'a [see vol. 8, p. 63].

**Fifth:** The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾ entered upon the meaning of the answer to a conditional, just as it entered in ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning: arise and warn, and arise and glorify your Lord. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zayd, so strike," meaning: strike Zayd, so the fa' is superfluous.

**Sixth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And purify your garments﴾. In it there are eight opinions. One of them is that what is meant by garments is deeds. The second is the heart. The third is the soul. The fourth is the body. The fifth is the family. The sixth is character. The seventh is religion. The eighth is the garments worn on the outside.

Whoever holds the first opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your deeds," as Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. Mansur narrated from Abu Razin, who said: It means "and your deeds, purify them." He said: When a man has bad deeds, they say "So-and-so has dirty garments," and when he has good deeds, they say "So-and-so has clean garments." Similar to this is reported from al-Suddi. From this is the saying of the poet:

O Allah, indeed Amir ibn Jahm,
or he performed Hajj in filthy garments.
[[Filthy garments: soiled with sins. In the editions: "or dham" with the letter dal, which is a corruption. The meaning of the verse: he performed Hajj while soiled with sins. Awdham al-hajj: he made the Hajj obligatory.]]

And from this is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: [A person will be resurrected in the two garments in which he died]. He meant his good deeds and bad deeds. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

Whoever holds the second opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your heart." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Their evidence is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

So take off my garments from your garments,
[[First half of the verse: "And if you were displeased with some disposition of mine."]]
meaning, my heart from your heart. Al-Mawardi said: They have two views on the interpretation of the verse. One: its meaning is "and purify your heart from sin and disobedience," as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. The second: "and purify your heart from treachery," meaning, do not betray, for then you would be someone with dirty garments. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, and he cited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

By the praise of Allah, I have not worn a garment of wickedness,
nor do I veil myself with treachery.

Whoever holds the third opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your soul," meaning from sins. The Arabs use garments as a metaphor for the soul, as said by Ibn Abbas. From this is the saying of Antara:

So I pierced with the long spear his garments,
the noble one is not forbidden from the spear-points.

And Imru' al-Qays said:
So take off my garments from your garments.

And [[The author attributed this verse later once to Ibn Abi Kabsha and once to Imru' al-Qays. In "al-Lisan" and "Sharh al-Qamus" it is attributed to Imru' al-Qays, but we have not found it in his diwan, and Ibn al-Arabi attributed it to Ibn Abi Kabsha. The last half-verse in the manuscripts is: "And their faces at gatherings are radiant."]] said:

The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces at the places of travel are bright,

meaning, the souls of the Banu Awf. Whoever holds the fourth opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your body," meaning from visible sins. Among what came from the Arabs in using garments as a metaphor for the body is the saying of Layla, when she mentioned camels:

They threw at them light garments, so you see
for them no likeness except the startled ostrich.

Its meaning: they rode them and threw them off by their own selves. As for those who held the fifth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your family, purify them from sins through admonition and discipline." The Arabs call the family a garment, a covering and a wrap. God Most High said: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

Al-Mawardi: For them there are two interpretations of the verse. The first: its meaning is "and your women, purify," by choosing chaste believing women. The second: enjoying them in the front passage and not the rear, in a state of purity and not during menstruation. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

As for those who held the sixth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your character, make good." This was said by al-Hasan and al-Qurazi, because a person's disposition encloses his states just as his garments enclose his self. The poet said:

"Yahya is not blamed for bad character,
and Yahya is pure of garments, free."

That is, of good character.

As for those who held the seventh opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your religion, purify." In the two Sahihs, from him (peace be upon him), he said: "I saw people with garments on them, some of which reached the breasts and some of which were below that, and I saw 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with a waist-wrap that he was dragging." They said: "O Messenger of God, how did you interpret that?" He said: "The religion."

Ibn Wahb related from Malik that he said: "I do not like to recite the Qur'an except in prayer and in mosques, not in the street." God Most High said: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾. Malik intends that he referred to garments by religion (by metonymy).

Abdullah ibn Nafi' related from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, from Malik ibn Anas, regarding His words Most High: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾, that means: do not wear them while treacherous. From this is the saying of Abu Kabsha [see note 3, p. 62 of this part]:

"The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces are white at travel, bright."

By the purity of their garments he means their safety from base acts; by the brightness of their faces their freedom from what is forbidden, or their beauty in creation, or both. This was said by Ibn al-Arabi.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: do not wear your garments over a lie, nor oppression, nor treachery, nor sin. This was said by Ikrima. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Or he blames, in garments, filthy ones."

That is, he has soiled them with sins.

Al-Nabigha said:

"Thin of sandals, fragrant are their waistwraps,
they are greeted with basil on the day of al-Sabasib."

[The verse is from a qasida in praise of Amr ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani. By "thin of sandals" he meant they are kings who do not patch their sandals, and by "fragrant of waistwraps" their chastity. "Garments of the Banu Awf, pure and clean."

The second: "and your garments, lift up and shorten," for shortening garments is further from impurity; when they trail on the ground there is no assurance that something will reach them that makes them impure. This was said by al-Zajjaj and Tawus. The third: "and your garments, purify from impurity with water." This was said by Muhammad ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and the jurists. The fourth: do not wear your garments except from lawful earnings, so that they are purified from the unlawful. It is related from Ibn Abbas: let not your garments that you wear be from an impure source of gain.

Ibn al-Arabi, having mentioned some of what we have mentioned, said: It is not impossible that the verse be taken in its general sense, both literal and figurative. If we take it to mean the known, clean garments, then it comprises two meanings. The first: shortening the hems, for if they are let loose they become soiled. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) said to a young man of the Ansar, when he saw his hem hanging loose: "Raise your waist-wrap, for it is more pious, cleaner and more lasting."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The waist-wrap of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no fault in what lies between that and the ankles, and whatever is below that is in the Fire." So the Prophet (ﷺ) made the limit of the waist-wrap at the ankles and threatened what is beneath it with the Fire. What is the matter with men who let their hems trail, lengthen their garments, and then labour to lift them with their hands? This is the state of pride and the cause of vanity. And the worst of the matter is that they disobey, become impure, and attach themselves to one with whom God has not associated anyone else nor joined anything else to Him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God does not look at the one who drags his garment in arrogance." The wording in the Sahih is: "Whoever drags his waist-wrap in arrogance, God will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, one side of my waist-wrap slips down unless I take care of it?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You are not among those who do it out of arrogance." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the prohibition general and excepted al-Siddiq. The lowly then wished to attach themselves to the exalted, but that is not for them.

The second meaning: washing them from impurity, which is evident from it and sound in it. Al-Mahdawi said: With it some scholars have argued for the obligation of the purity of the garment. Ibn Sirin and Ibn Zayd said: do not pray except in a pure garment. Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence for the obligation of the garment's purity, whereas according to Malik and the people of Madina it is not an obligation, and likewise the purity of the body. What indicates this is the consensus on the permissibility of prayer after cleaning with stones without washing. This matter has been discussed fully in Surat al-Bara'a [see vol. 8, p. 63].

The Chapter of al-Muddaththir (The Cloaked One) is Meccan, according to all scholars. It has fifty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn, and glorify your Lord, and purify your garments.﴾

There are six issues in this verse.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, meaning, O you who has wrapped himself in his garments, that is, covered himself with them and slept. Its original form is al-mutadaththir, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* because they are similar (in articulation). Ubayy read "al-mutadaththir" according to the original form. Muqatil said: most of this chapter concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who was one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and who used to narrate, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, while narrating about the interruption of revelation, and he said in his hadith: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky, so I raised my head, and behold, the angel who had come to me at Hira was sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was seized with terror [[ji'tu means: I was alarmed and frightened.]] by him, so I returned and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols﴾ (in another narration: before the prayer was made obligatory, and they are the idols). He said: 'Then the revelation followed in succession.'" Al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

Muslim said: Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to us, he said: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, he said: al-Awza'i narrated to us, he said: I heard Yahya say: I asked Abu Salama: "Which Qur'an was revealed first?" He said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾." I said: "Or 'Read'?" He said: "I asked Jabir ibn Abdullah which Qur'an was revealed first, and he said: '﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾.' I said: 'Or "Read"?' Jabir said: 'I will tell you what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us: He said: "I stayed in seclusion at Hira for a month. When I finished my seclusion, I descended and went into the valley's bottom, and I was called. I looked before me, behind me, to my right and to my left, and saw no one. Then I was called again, and I looked and saw no one. Then I was called again, so I raised my head, and behold, he was on the throne in the air," meaning Jibril ﷺ. "A violent trembling seized me, so I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up and poured water over me. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments.﴾"" (al-Bukhari transmitted it, and in it he said:) "I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up and pour cold water over me.' So they wrapped me up and poured cold water over me, and this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols. And do not give to receive more.﴾"

Ibn al-Arabi said: Some exegetes have said that something happened to the Prophet ﷺ from Uqba [ibn Rabi'a [[The addition is from Ibn al-Arabi.]]], so he returned to his home grieved, became agitated and lay down, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. This is false.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: It was said that the statement of the disbelievers of Mecca, "You are a sorcerer," reached him, and he felt grief from that and became feverish, so he wrapped himself in his garments. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, do not dwell on their words, and convey the message to them. It was also said: Abu Lahab, Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-As ibn Wa'il and Mut'im ibn Adi gathered and said: "The delegations of the Arabs have gathered during the days of the Hajj, and they ask one another about the matter of Muhammad, and you have disagreed in reporting about him. One says he is mad, another says he is a soothsayer, another says he is a poet, and the Arabs know that all of this does not combine in one man. So name Muhammad with one name on which they can agree, and the Arabs will call him by it." A man among them stood and said: "A poet." Al-Walid said: "I have heard the speech of Ibn al-Abras and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and the speech of Muhammad does not resemble the speech of either of them." They said: "A soothsayer." He said: "A soothsayer speaks truth and lies, and Muhammad has never lied at all." Another stood and said: "A madman." Al-Walid said: "The madman chokes people, and Muhammad has never choked anyone at all." Al-Walid returned to his house, and they said: "al-Walid ibn al-Mughira has turned away." Abu Jahl entered upon him and said: "What is wrong with you, O Abu Abd Shams? These are the Quraysh gathering something for you, which they will give you. They claim that you are in need and have turned away." Al-Walid said: "I have no need for that, but I thought about Muhammad, and I said: What is the sorcerer's work?" It was said: "He separates the father from his son, the brother from his brother, and the woman from her husband." I said: "He is a sorcerer." This spread among the people, and they began to shout: "Muhammad is a sorcerer." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to his house grieved, and he wrapped himself in a qatifa (a thick cloak), and ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed.

Ikrima said: The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: the one wrapped in prophethood and its burdens. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a distant metaphor, because he had not yet been made a prophet. And also, since this was the first of the Qur'an, he had not yet become accustomed to it, after it had been the second thing revealed.

**Second:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is a gentle address from the Generous to the Beloved, since He called him by his state and described him by his attribute, and did not say "O Muhammad" or "O so-and-so," so that he would feel softness and gentleness from his Lord, as has been mentioned previously in the chapter of al-Muzzammil. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Ali when he slept in the mosque: "Arise, O Abu Turab (father of dust)." He had gone out angry at Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, so his cloak fell off and dust touched him. Muslim transmitted it. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to Hudhayfa on the night of the Trench: "Arise, O sleeper," and this has been mentioned before.

**Third:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, frighten the people of Mecca and warn them of punishment if they do not submit. It was said: warning here means informing them of his prophethood, because it is the prelude to the message. It was said: it is calling them to monotheism, because that is its purpose. Al-Farra' said: Arise and pray, and command others to pray.

**Fourth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, your master, your owner, and the one who sets your affairs right, so magnify Him, and describe Him as greater than having a consort or a son. It is reported in a hadith that they said: "With what should we begin the prayer?" So this was revealed: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, describe Him as greatest. Ibn al-Arabi said: Although this statement, by its generality, requires the takbir of prayer, what is meant by it is the takbir [[As in Ahkam al-Quran, the Cairo edition of Ibn al-Arabi's commentary, 1331 AH. It has been narrated that Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalted is Hubal!" and the Prophet ﷺ said: [Say: Allah is higher and more majestic]. This expression has become, by the usage of the Shari'a, the takbir of all acts of worship, adhan, prayer and remembrance, with the words "Allahu Akbar." The words of the Prophet ﷺ that came in an absolute form were interpreted in that sense in several contexts, among them his saying: [Its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam]. Among its contexts are the times of uttering the name over slaughtered animals for Allah, to single Him out from polytheism, to proclaim His name in sacrifice, and to single out what He has legislated for His command to shed blood.

Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, one side of my waist-wrap slips down unless I take care of it?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You are not among those who do it out of arrogance." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the prohibition general and excepted al-Siddiq. The lowly then wished to attach themselves to the exalted, but that is not for them.

The second meaning: washing them from impurity, which is evident from it and sound in it. Al-Mahdawi said: With it some scholars have argued for the obligation of the purity of the garment. Ibn Sirin and Ibn Zayd said: do not pray except in a pure garment. Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence for the obligation of the garment's purity, whereas according to Malik and the people of Madina it is not an obligation, and likewise the purity of the body. What indicates this is the consensus on the permissibility of prayer after cleaning with stones without washing. This matter has been discussed fully in Surat al-Bara'a [see vol. 8, p. 63].

The Chapter of al-Muddaththir (The Cloaked One) is Meccan, according to all scholars. It has fifty-six verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who are wrapped up, arise and warn, and glorify your Lord, and purify your garments.﴾

There are six issues in this verse.

**First:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾, meaning, O you who has wrapped himself in his garments, that is, covered himself with them and slept. Its original form is al-mutadaththir, and the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* because they are similar (in articulation). Ubayy read "al-mutadaththir" according to the original form. Muqatil said: most of this chapter concerns al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.

In Sahih Muslim, from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who was one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and who used to narrate, he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, while narrating about the interruption of revelation, and he said in his hadith: "While I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky, so I raised my head, and behold, the angel who had come to me at Hira was sitting on a chair between the sky and the earth."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was seized with terror [[ji'tu means: I was alarmed and frightened.]] by him, so I returned and said: 'Wrap me up, wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols﴾ (in another narration: before the prayer was made obligatory, and they are the idols). He said: 'Then the revelation followed in succession.'" Al-Tirmidhi also transmitted it and said: "A hasan sahih hadith."

Muslim said: Zuhayr ibn Harb narrated to us, he said: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, he said: al-Awza'i narrated to us, he said: I heard Yahya say: I asked Abu Salama: "Which Qur'an was revealed first?" He said: "﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾." I said: "Or 'Read'?" He said: "I asked Jabir ibn Abdullah which Qur'an was revealed first, and he said: '﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾.' I said: 'Or "Read"?' Jabir said: 'I will tell you what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ told us: He said: "I stayed in seclusion at Hira for a month. When I finished my seclusion, I descended and went into the valley's bottom, and I was called. I looked before me, behind me, to my right and to my left, and saw no one. Then I was called again, and I looked and saw no one. Then I was called again, so I raised my head, and behold, he was on the throne in the air," meaning Jibril ﷺ. "A violent trembling seized me, so I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up,' and they wrapped me up and poured water over me. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments.﴾"" (al-Bukhari transmitted it, and in it he said:) "I came to Khadija and said: 'Wrap me up and pour cold water over me.' So they wrapped me up and poured cold water over me, and this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up. Arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments. And shun the idols. And do not give to receive more.﴾"

Ibn al-Arabi said: Some exegetes have said that something happened to the Prophet ﷺ from Uqba [ibn Rabi'a [[The addition is from Ibn al-Arabi.]]], so he returned to his home grieved, became agitated and lay down, and then this was revealed: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾. This is false.

Al-Qushayri Abu Nasr said: It was said that the statement of the disbelievers of Mecca, "You are a sorcerer," reached him, and he felt grief from that and became feverish, so he wrapped himself in his garments. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, do not dwell on their words, and convey the message to them. It was also said: Abu Lahab, Abu Sufyan, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayya ibn Khalaf, al-As ibn Wa'il and Mut'im ibn Adi gathered and said: "The delegations of the Arabs have gathered during the days of the Hajj, and they ask one another about the matter of Muhammad, and you have disagreed in reporting about him. One says he is mad, another says he is a soothsayer, another says he is a poet, and the Arabs know that all of this does not combine in one man. So name Muhammad with one name on which they can agree, and the Arabs will call him by it." A man among them stood and said: "A poet." Al-Walid said: "I have heard the speech of Ibn al-Abras and Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and the speech of Muhammad does not resemble the speech of either of them." They said: "A soothsayer." He said: "A soothsayer speaks truth and lies, and Muhammad has never lied at all." Another stood and said: "A madman." Al-Walid said: "The madman chokes people, and Muhammad has never choked anyone at all." Al-Walid returned to his house, and they said: "al-Walid ibn al-Mughira has turned away." Abu Jahl entered upon him and said: "What is wrong with you, O Abu Abd Shams? These are the Quraysh gathering something for you, which they will give you. They claim that you are in need and have turned away." Al-Walid said: "I have no need for that, but I thought about Muhammad, and I said: What is the sorcerer's work?" It was said: "He separates the father from his son, the brother from his brother, and the woman from her husband." I said: "He is a sorcerer." This spread among the people, and they began to shout: "Muhammad is a sorcerer." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to his house grieved, and he wrapped himself in a qatifa (a thick cloak), and ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ was revealed.

Ikrima said: The meaning of ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is: the one wrapped in prophethood and its burdens. Ibn al-Arabi said: This is a distant metaphor, because he had not yet been made a prophet. And also, since this was the first of the Qur'an, he had not yet become accustomed to it, after it had been the second thing revealed.

**Second:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ is a gentle address from the Generous to the Beloved, since He called him by his state and described him by his attribute, and did not say "O Muhammad" or "O so-and-so," so that he would feel softness and gentleness from his Lord, as has been mentioned previously in the chapter of al-Muzzammil. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Ali when he slept in the mosque: "Arise, O Abu Turab (father of dust)." He had gone out angry at Fatima, may Allah be pleased with her, so his cloak fell off and dust touched him. Muslim transmitted it. Similar to it is the saying of the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to Hudhayfa on the night of the Trench: "Arise, O sleeper," and this has been mentioned before.

**Third:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning, frighten the people of Mecca and warn them of punishment if they do not submit. It was said: warning here means informing them of his prophethood, because it is the prelude to the message. It was said: it is calling them to monotheism, because that is its purpose. Al-Farra' said: Arise and pray, and command others to pray.

**Fourth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, your master, your owner, and the one who sets your affairs right, so magnify Him, and describe Him as greater than having a consort or a son. It is reported in a hadith that they said: "With what should we begin the prayer?" So this was revealed: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾, meaning, describe Him as greatest. Ibn al-Arabi said: Although this statement, by its generality, requires the takbir of prayer, what is meant by it is the takbir [[As in Ahkam al-Quran, the Cairo edition of Ibn al-Arabi's commentary, 1331 AH. In what the author quoted from Ibn al-Arabi here there is alteration of wording with addition and omission; it should be consulted, vol. 2, p. 287.]], and the sanctification and transcendence, by rejecting rivals and idols besides Him, not taking any protector other than Him, not worshipping anything other than Him, not seeing any act for anyone other than Him, and no blessing except from Him.

It has been narrated that Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalted is Hubal!" and the Prophet ﷺ said: [Say: Allah is higher and more majestic]. This expression has become, by the usage of the Shari'a, the takbir of all acts of worship, adhan, prayer and remembrance, with the words "Allahu Akbar." The words of the Prophet ﷺ that came in an absolute form were interpreted in that sense in several contexts, among them his saying: [Its opening is the takbir, and its closing is the salam]. The Shari'a in its usage requires what its generality requires. Among its contexts are the times of uttering the name over slaughtered animals for Allah, to single Him out from polytheism, to proclaim His name in sacrifice, and to single out what He has legislated for His command to shed blood.

I say: It has already been mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara [[See vol. 1, p. 175.]] that this expression, "Allahu Akbar," is the one by which worship is performed in prayer, transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ. In the exegesis: when Allah's saying, exalted is He, ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood and said: [Allahu Akbar]. Then Khadija said the takbir, and she knew that it was revelation from Allah, exalted is He. Al-Qushayri mentioned it.

**Fifth:** The fa' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And glorify your Lord﴾ entered upon the meaning of the answer to a conditional, just as it entered in ﴿Arise and warn﴾, meaning: arise and warn, and arise and glorify your Lord. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Jinni said: It is like your saying: "Zayd, so strike," meaning: strike Zayd, so the fa' is superfluous.

**Sixth:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And purify your garments﴾. In it there are eight opinions. One of them is that what is meant by garments is deeds. The second is the heart. The third is the soul. The fourth is the body. The fifth is the family. The sixth is character. The seventh is religion. The eighth is the garments worn on the outside.

Whoever holds the first opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your deeds," as Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said. Mansur narrated from Abu Razin, who said: It means "and your deeds, purify them." He said: When a man has bad deeds, they say "So-and-so has dirty garments," and when he has good deeds, they say "So-and-so has clean garments." Similar to this is reported from al-Suddi. From this is the saying of the poet:

O Allah, indeed Amir ibn Jahm,
or he performed Hajj in filthy garments.
[[Filthy garments: soiled with sins. In the editions: "or dham" with the letter dal, which is a corruption. The meaning of the verse: he performed Hajj while soiled with sins. Awdham al-hajj: he made the Hajj obligatory.]]

And from this is what is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: [A person will be resurrected in the two garments in which he died]. He meant his good deeds and bad deeds. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

Whoever holds the second opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your heart." This was said by Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Their evidence is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

So take off my garments from your garments,
[[First half of the verse: "And if you were displeased with some disposition of mine."]]
meaning, my heart from your heart. Al-Mawardi said: They have two views on the interpretation of the verse. One: its meaning is "and purify your heart from sin and disobedience," as said by Ibn Abbas and Qatada. The second: "and purify your heart from treachery," meaning, do not betray, for then you would be someone with dirty garments. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, and he cited the saying of Ghaylan ibn Salama al-Thaqafi:

By the praise of Allah, I have not worn a garment of wickedness,
nor do I veil myself with treachery.

Whoever holds the third opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your soul," meaning from sins. The Arabs use garments as a metaphor for the soul, as said by Ibn Abbas. From this is the saying of Antara:

So I pierced with the long spear his garments,
the noble one is not forbidden from the spear-points.

And Imru' al-Qays said:
So take off my garments from your garments.

And [[The author attributed this verse later once to Ibn Abi Kabsha and once to Imru' al-Qays. In "al-Lisan" and "Sharh al-Qamus" it is attributed to Imru' al-Qays, but we have not found it in his diwan, and Ibn al-Arabi attributed it to Ibn Abi Kabsha. The last half-verse in the manuscripts is: "And their faces at gatherings are radiant."]] said:

The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces at the places of travel are bright,

meaning, the souls of the Banu Awf. Whoever holds the fourth opinion says: the interpretation of the verse is "and purify your body," meaning from visible sins. Among what came from the Arabs in using garments as a metaphor for the body is the saying of Layla, when she mentioned camels:

They threw at them light garments, so you see
for them no likeness except the startled ostrich.

Its meaning: they rode them and threw them off by their own selves. As for those who held the fifth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your family, purify them from sins through admonition and discipline." The Arabs call the family a garment, a covering and a wrap. God Most High said: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 187].

Al-Mawardi: For them there are two interpretations of the verse. The first: its meaning is "and your women, purify," by choosing chaste believing women. The second: enjoying them in the front passage and not the rear, in a state of purity and not during menstruation. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

As for those who held the sixth opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your character, make good." This was said by al-Hasan and al-Qurazi, because a person's disposition encloses his states just as his garments enclose his self. The poet said:

"Yahya is not blamed for bad character,
and Yahya is pure of garments, free."

That is, of good character.

As for those who held the seventh opinion, they said: the interpretation of the verse is "and your religion, purify." In the two Sahihs, from him (peace be upon him), he said: "I saw people with garments on them, some of which reached the breasts and some of which were below that, and I saw 'Umar ibn al-Khattab with a waist-wrap that he was dragging." They said: "O Messenger of God, how did you interpret that?" He said: "The religion."

Ibn Wahb related from Malik that he said: "I do not like to recite the Qur'an except in prayer and in mosques, not in the street." God Most High said: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾. Malik intends that he referred to garments by religion (by metonymy).

Abdullah ibn Nafi' related from Abu Bakr ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Abd Allah ibn Umar ibn al-Khattab, from Malik ibn Anas, regarding His words Most High: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾, that means: do not wear them while treacherous. From this is the saying of Abu Kabsha [see note 3, p. 62 of this part]:

"The garments of the Banu Awf are pure and clean,
and their faces are white at travel, bright."

By the purity of their garments he means their safety from base acts; by the brightness of their faces their freedom from what is forbidden, or their beauty in creation, or both. This was said by Ibn al-Arabi.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna said: do not wear your garments over a lie, nor oppression, nor treachery, nor sin. This was said by Ikrima. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Or he blames, in garments, filthy ones."

That is, he has soiled them with sins.

Al-Nabigha said:

"Thin of sandals, fragrant are their waistwraps,
they are greeted with basil on the day of al-Sabasib."

[The verse is from a qasida in praise of Amr ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani. By "thin of sandals" he meant they are kings who do not patch their sandals, and by "fragrant of waistwraps" their chastity. Al-Sabasib is the day of Palm Sunday (al-Sha'anin), a feast day for the Christians, and the one praised was a Christian.]

As for those who held the eighth opinion, they said: the intended meaning is the garments worn. They have four interpretations of it. The first: its meaning is "and your garments, cleanse." From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Garments of the Banu Awf, pure and clean."

The second: "and your garments, lift up and shorten," for shortening garments is further from impurity; when they trail on the ground there is no assurance that something will reach them that makes them impure. This was said by al-Zajjaj and Tawus. The third: "and your garments, purify from impurity with water." This was said by Muhammad ibn Sirin, Ibn Zayd and the jurists. The fourth: do not wear your garments except from lawful earnings, so that they are purified from the unlawful. It is related from Ibn Abbas: let not your garments that you wear be from an impure source of gain.

Ibn al-Arabi, having mentioned some of what we have mentioned, said: It is not impossible that the verse be taken in its general sense, both literal and figurative. If we take it to mean the known, clean garments, then it comprises two meanings. The first: shortening the hems, for if they are let loose they become soiled. For this reason 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him) said to a young man of the Ansar, when he saw his hem hanging loose: "Raise your waist-wrap, for it is more pious, cleaner and more lasting."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also said: "The waist-wrap of the believer reaches to the middle of his shins; there is no fault in what lies between that and the ankles, and whatever is below that is in the Fire." So the Prophet (ﷺ) made the limit of the waist-wrap at the ankles and threatened what is beneath it with the Fire. What is the matter with men who let their hems trail, lengthen their garments, and then labour to lift them with their hands? This is the state of pride and the cause of vanity. And the worst of the matter is that they disobey, become impure, and attach themselves to one with whom God has not associated anyone else nor joined anything else to Him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God does not look at the one who drags his garment in arrogance." The wording in the Sahih is: "Whoever drags his waist-wrap in arrogance, God will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection." Abu Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, one side of my waist-wrap slips down unless I take care of it?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "You are not among those who do it out of arrogance." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made the prohibition general and excepted al-Siddiq. The lowly then wished to attach themselves to the exalted, but that is not for them.

The second meaning: washing them from impurity, which is evident from it and sound in it. Al-Mahdawi said: With it some scholars have argued for the obligation of the purity of the garment. Ibn Sirin and Ibn Zayd said: do not pray except in a pure garment. Al-Shafi'i used it as evidence for the obligation of the garment's purity, whereas according to Malik and the people of Madina it is not an obligation, and likewise the purity of the body. What indicates this is the consensus on the permissibility of prayer after cleaning with stones without washing. This matter has been discussed fully in Surat al-Bara'a [see vol. 8, p. 63].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the abomination, forsake﴾. Mujahid and Ikrimah said: it means the idols. Its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd said likewise. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas also: ﴿and sin, forsake﴾, that is, abandon it. Likewise Mughira narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "al-Rujz" is sin. Qatadah said: al-Rujz refers to Isaf and Na'ila, two idols that were beside the House (the Ka'bah). It was also said: al-Rujz means punishment, with the omission of a modifier (idafah) understood, the meaning being: "and the deed of al-rujz, forsake," or "the deed that leads to punishment." The root meaning of al-rujz is punishment. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿If You remove from us the punishment (al-rijz), we will certainly believe in You﴾ [al-A'raf: 134]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We sent upon them a punishment (rijzan) from the sky﴾ [al-A'raf: 162]. Thus the idols were named rujz because they lead to punishment.

The common reading is (al-rijz) with a kasra on the ra'. Al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hafs from 'Asim read (al-rujz) with a damma on the ra', and both are dialectal variants, like al-dhikr and al-dhukr. Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi' and al-Kisa'i said: al-rujz with a damma means the idol, and with a kasra means impurity and disobedience. Al-Kisa'i also said: with a damma it means the idol, and with a kasra it means punishment. As-Suddi said: "al-rujz" with a fathah on the ra' means the threat [[The phrase "with a fathah on the ra' ..." is as it appears in all copies of the original text, and we have not found it in the references available to us.]].

There are three issues concerning this verse.

The first concerns His saying, exalted is He: "And do not bestow favour in order to gain more" (74:6). Regarding it there are eleven interpretations (ta'wilat).

The first: Do not bestow favour upon your Lord because of the burdens of prophethood that you bear, like one who considers excessive what he bears on account of others.

The second: Do not give a gift seeking something better in return. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and Qatadah. Al-Dahhak said: "This was forbidden by Allah to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he was commanded with the noblest manners and the most exalted ethics, and He permitted it to his community." Mujahid also said this.

The third: also from Mujahid: Do not weaken (la tadha'if) in the matter of doing much good. From your saying "habl matin" (a weak rope) when it is feeble. Its evidence is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa la tamnun tastakthir min al-khayr" (and do not bestow favour, you who seek to increase in good).

The fourth: also from Mujahid and al-Rabi': Do not magnify your deed in your eyes, so that you seek to increase in good, for it is among the blessings Allah has bestowed upon you. Ibn Kaysan said: Do not consider your deed great, so that you see it as coming from yourself; rather your deed is a favour (minnah) from Allah upon you, since He made a path for you to His worship.

The fifth: al-Hasan said: Do not bestow favour upon Allah through your deed, so that you consider it great.

The sixth: Do not bestow favour through prophethood and the Qur'an upon people, so that you take from them a reward by which you increase.

The seventh: al-Qurazi said: Do not give your wealth as a bribe for flattery (musana'ah).

The eighth: Zayd ibn Aslam said: When you give a gift, give it for your Lord.

The ninth: Do not say, "I supplicated, but I was not answered."

The tenth: Do not perform an act of obedience while seeking its reward; rather be patient until Allah is the One who rewards you for it.

The eleventh: Do not do good in order to be seen by people.

The second issue: Although these sayings are all intended, the most evident of them is the statement of Ibn 'Abbas: "Do not give in order to take back more than you gave of wealth." It is said: "I bestowed upon so-and-so such-and-such" (mantu fulanan kadhha), meaning I gave him. A gift is also called minnah. It is as if he was commanded that his gifts be for Allah, not for expecting a return from creation upon them, because he, peace be upon him, did not amass worldly goods. For this reason he said: "Of what Allah has granted you as spoils, I have nothing except the fifth, and the fifth is returned to you." Whatever remained of the provision for his household was spent on the interests of the Muslims. For this reason he left no inheritance, because he did not allow himself to hoard or acquire. Allah, exalted is He, protected him from desire for anything of the world. For this reason charity (sadaqah) was forbidden to him, while gifts (hadiyyah) were permitted to him; he would accept them and reciprocate. He said: "If I were invited to a trotter (kura'), I would accept, and if a foreleg (dhira') were presented to me, I would accept it." Ibn al-'Arabi: He accepted them as a sunnah and did not regard them as excessive in law. If he did not give a gift in order to gain more, then the wealthy are more deserving of avoiding it, for it is a door of humiliation. Likewise the saying of whoever says its meaning is: do not give a gift while expecting its reward, for expectation is attachment to desires, and that is in its place a matter of prohibition. Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given pairs of them to enjoy, the splendour of the worldly life, that We may test them therein; but the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting" (20:131). This is permissible for all creatures, because it belongs to the enjoyment of this world, and the seeking of gain and multiplication through it. As for the one who said it means the deed, i.e., do not bestow favour upon Allah by your deed so that you consider it great, this is correct, for if a son of Adam obeyed Allah his whole life without slackening, he would not reach even part of the gratitude due for Allah's blessings.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: "And do not bestow favour" (wa la tamnun). The common reading is with the doubled letter shown (idhhar al-tadh'if). Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi, Ashhab al-'Uqayli and al-Hasan read "wa la tamunn" with idgham and a fatha. "Tastakthir" in the common reading is in the nominative (raf'), and it has the meaning of a circumstantial clause (hal), as you say: "Zayd came running" (jaa Zaydun yarkudu), meaning running. That is, do not give anything, presuming that you will take in its place what is more than it. Al-Hasan read it in the jussive (jazm) as a response to the prohibition, which is weak, because it is not a true response. It may also be a substitution (badal) for "tamnun", as if he said: "do not seek increase." Abu Hatim rejected this and said: because bestowing favour is not the same as seeking increase, so it cannot be substituted for it. It may be that the vowel was dropped for lightness, like 'adhd, or that the pause form is taken into account. Al-A'mash and Yahya read "tastakthira" with a fatha, assuming the lam of purpose (lam kay), as if he said: "and do not bestow favour in order that you may increase." It is also said that it is with an implied "an" (that), as in the saying: [The line of Tarafah ibn al-'Abd from his Mu'allaqah, whose completion is: "And that I witness pleasures, will you be made eternal for me?"]: "Ala ayyuha al-zajiri ahdhur al-wagha" (Ah, you who restrain me from attending the battle). This is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading: "wa la tamnun an tastakthira." Al-Kisa'i said: When "an" is dropped, it takes the nominative, and the meaning is the same. The bestowing of favour may also mean enumerating the favours upon the one who has been favoured, and so it returns to the second saying, and the verse of Allah, exalted is He, supports it: "Do not render your charities void by reminding and harming" (2:264). It may also be intended in this verse. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for your Lord, be patient﴾, meaning: and for your Master and Owner, be patient in performing His obligations and His worship. Mujahid said: "Be patient over what you have been made to suffer" [[In manuscripts A, H and L: "what you were made to convey" (ma udîtu → ma ublagh)]]. Ibn Zayd said: "You have been charged with a great matter, fighting the Arabs and the non-Arabs, so be patient in it for the sake of God." It has also been said: "Be patient under the decrees of destiny for the sake of God, exalted is He." It has also been said: "Be patient in trials, for He tests His friends and chosen servants." It has also been said: "Be patient in His commands and His prohibitions." It has also been said: "Be patient in separation from family and homeland."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 8–10:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Then when the trumpet is sounded (nuqira fi al-naqur)﴾. That is, when the Trumpet (al-sur) is blown. Al-Naqur is fa'ul from al-naqr, as if it is that into which something is blown (yunqar fihi) for producing a sound. Al-naqr in the speech of the Arabs means the sound, and from it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"I lower him with the naqr when I have risen over him... and he raises a glance, not hidden, lowered."

And they say: naqqara bi-ism al-rajul, when he called the man by his name, singling him out with his call. Mujahid and others said: it is like the shape of a horn (buq), and by it is meant the second blast. It was said: the first, because it is the beginning of the great, overwhelming severity. The discussion of this has already been covered in full in "al-Naml" [[See vol. 13, p. 339.]] and "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 30.]] and in the book "al-Tadhkira", praise be to Allah. And from Abu Hibban, who said: Zurara ibn Awfa led us in prayer, and when he reached ﴿Then when the trumpet is sounded in the naqur﴾, he fell down dead.

(﴿That, on that Day, will be a difficult Day﴾) That is, that Day is a severe day (﴿for the disbelievers﴾), that is, for whoever disbelieved in Allah and His prophets, peace be upon them (﴿not easy﴾), that is, not light and not trivial. This is because their knots are not untied except into a knot that is harder than it. Unlike the believing monotheists who sin, for their knots are untied into what is lighter, until they enter Paradise by the mercy of Allah, the Exalted. And (﴿yawma'idhin﴾) is in the accusative by the estimate of: "That is a difficult day, on that day." It was said: it is in the genitive by estimating a preposition whose meaning is: "That is in that day." It was said: it may be in the nominative, but it is built on the fathah because it is attached to a non-declinable word.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 74, verses 11–17:**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Leave me with the one whom I created alone﴾. (*Dharni*) means "leave me." It is a word of warning and threat. "Whom I created" means: leave me and the one whom I created alone. On this reading, *wahidan* ("alone") is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) referring back to the omitted object pronoun, meaning: I created him alone, with no wealth and no children, and then I gave him what I gave him.

The exegetes hold that the person meant is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, although all people were created in the same way as he was. He was singled out for mention because he was distinguished by his ingratitude for blessings and by harming the Messenger (peace be upon him). He was called "the Lone One" among his people. Ibn Abbas said: al-Walid used to say, "I am the lone one, son of the lone one. I have no equal among the Arabs, and Abu al-Mughira has no equal." He was called "the Lone One," so God the Exalted said: "Leave me with the one whom I created alone," according to his own claim, not that God confirmed that he was alone.

Some said that the Exalted's words *wahidan* refer to the Lord, the Exalted, with two meanings. The first: "Leave me alone with him, for I will requite him in taking vengeance against him more than any avenger." The second: "I have been singular (*infaradtu*; in manuscripts A, H and W: *uftirdtu*) in creating him, and no one shared that with me, so I will destroy him and I need no helper in destroying him." On this reading, *wahidan* is a *hal* referring to the subject pronoun, the *ta'* in *khalaqtu* ("I created"). The first view is the opinion of Mujahid: "I created him alone in his mother's womb, with no wealth and no children, then I bestowed blessings on him and he disbelieved." On this view, the phrase *wahidan* refers back to al-Walid, meaning he had nothing, and then I gave him wealth. It was also said: he meant by this to show that he will be raised alone as he was created alone. It was also said: *al-wahid* is the one whose father is not known. Al-Walid was known to be an adopted child (*da'iyy*), as we have mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Violent, and after that, of doubtful birth﴾ [al-Qalam: 13], and that verse also describes al-Walid.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And I gave him abundant wealth﴾. That is: I gave him sustenance and bestowed upon him abundant wealth. This consisted of what al-Walid owned between Mecca and al-Ta'if of camels, *hujur* (the plural of *hujra*, which means a female horse), livestock, gardens, male slaves and female slaves. Thus Ibn Abbas used to say. Mujahid said: the yield was a thousand dinars. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Abbas also said this. Qatada said: six thousand dinars. Sufyan al-Thawri and Qatada said: four thousand dinars. Al-Thawri also said: a million dinars. Muqatil said: he had an orchard whose produce never ceased, in winter or in summer. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "And I gave him abundant wealth" refers to a yield from month to month. Al-Nu'man ibn Salim said: land on which he planted crops. Al-Qushayri said: the most apparent meaning is a reference to a provision that does not cease but continues, such as crops, livestock and trade.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And sons present (*shuhudan*)﴾. That is: present, who were never absent from him in his affairs. Mujahid and Qatada said: they were ten. It was also said: twelve, as said by al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. Al-Dahhak said: seven were born in Mecca and five were born in al-Ta'if. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they were thirteen sons. Muqatil said: they were seven, all of them men, and three of them became Muslims: Khalid, Hisham and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. He said: after the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to lose from his wealth and his children until he died. It was also said: *shuhudan* means that when he was mentioned, they were mentioned along with him; this is what Ibn Abbas said. It was also said: *shuhudan* means that they had become like him in being present for what he used to attend, and in carrying out what he used to handle. The first view is the opinion of al-Suddi, meaning present in Mecca, not travelling away from him for trade and not absent.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And I spread out for him a wide spreading﴾. That is: I spread out his livelihood widely, so that he remained in his town, at peace and in luxury, and people deferred to his opinion. *Tamhid* (spreading out) in the speech of the Arabs means preparing and readying, and from it comes *mahd al-sabiyy* (the cradle of a child). Ibn Abbas said: "And I spread out for him a wide spreading" means I extended for him what lies between Yemen and Syria. Mujahid also said this. It is also reported from Mujahid concerning "a wide spreading" that it means wealth piled upon wealth, as a bed is spread out.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then he desires that I should increase (more)﴾. That is: after all of this, al-Walid still desires that I should increase him in wealth and children.

﴿Nay!﴾ That is: it will not happen with his ingratitude for blessings. Al-Hasan and others said: meaning, then he desires that I admit him to Paradise. Al-Walid used to say: "If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me." So God the Exalted replied to him and refuted him, saying: "Nay!" That is: I will not increase him. He continued to see loss in his wealth and his children until he died.

The *thumma* in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Then he desires﴾, is not the *thumma* of sequence (*al-nasaq*) but of wonder, and it is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 1]. This is like when you say: "I gave you, then you shun me," as one who is astonished at that. It was also said: he desires that I leave this to his descendants, because he used to say: "Muhammad is cut off (*mabtur*), that is, he is without descendants, and his mention will end with his death." He thought that what he had been given would not cease with his death. It was also said: he desires that I help him against his disbelief.

*Nay* (*kalla*) is a cutting off of hope regarding what he desired of increase, so it is connected to the earlier speech. It was also said: *kalla* means "truly," and it begins a new statement. ﴿Indeed, he was hostile to Our signs (*'anidan*)﴾, that is, al-Walid was an opponent of the Prophet (peace be upon him) and of what he brought. It is said: *'anid* (one who opposes) and *'anid* are like *jalis* (sitting) and *jalis* (companion). This was said by Mujahid. *'Anada* (in the form *ya'nidu*, with a kasra) means he opposed and rejected the truth while knowing it, so he is *'anid* and *'anid*. The *'anid* is the camel that turns aside from the path and departs from the straight course, and its plural is *'unnad*, like *rakI'* and *rukka'*. Abu Ubayda recited the verse of al-Harithi:

When you ride, make me the middle one... Indeed I am old and cannot bear the stubborn ones.

Abu Salih said: *'anid* means "one who keeps away," and the poet said:

Our state is one that separates us, a distant separation, indeed parting is stubborn.

Qatada said: *jahidan* (one who denies). Muqatil said: *mu'ridan* (one who turns away). Ibn Abbas said: *jahudan* (one who ungratefully denies). It was also said: he is the one who openly transgresses. It is also reported from Mujahid that he said: "one who stands aside from the truth, opposes it and turns away from it." All these meanings are close to one another. The Arabs say: "*'anada* the man" when he transgresses and exceeds his limit. The *'anud* among camels is the one that does not mix with the camels but stays on its own. A man is *'anud* if he stays alone and does not mix with people. The *'anid* means one who is tyrannical. A vein is *'annid* if its blood does not stop flowing. All of this is one analogy, and it has already been discussed in Surat Ibrahim [see vol. 9, p. 349]. The plural of *'anid* is *'unud*, like *raghif* and *rughuf*.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿I will drive him to a steep ascent (*sa'ud*)﴾. That is: I will burden him. Ibn Abbas used to say: "I will compel him." In the speech of the Arabs, *irhaq* means that a person is forced to something. *Sa'ud*: a mountain of fire upon which he climbs for seventy autumns, then falls down in the same way forever. This was narrated by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri from the Prophet (ﷺ), and al-Tirmidhi reported it and said: "It is a gharib (unusual) hadith." Atiyya narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: "It is a rock in Hell. When they place their hands on it, it melts, and when they lift them, it returns. It takes forty years to reach its top. He is pulled from the front with chains and struck from behind with iron maces, until when he reaches its top he is thrown down to its bottom, and that is his perpetual condition." This meaning has already been mentioned in Surat Qul Uhiya [al-Jinn; see p. 28 of this part]. In the tafsir it is said: it is a smooth rock that he is compelled to climb. When he reaches its top, he is cast down into Hell, and he then falls for a thousand years before he reaches the bottom of Hell, burning seventy times every day, and then he is recreated anew. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning is "I will burden him with a hardship of punishment, with no rest in it." Al-Hasan and Qatada said similarly. It was also said: he will be made to climb his own soul to the point of the death-rattle, even if death does not follow it, so that he is punished from within his body as he is punished from outside it.

He said: after the revelation of this verse, al-Walid continued to lose from his wealth and his children until he died.
