Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 18–25:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated﴾. He means al-Walid. He reflected upon the matter of the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an, and "calculated" means he prepared the speech in his own mind. The Arabs say: "I qadartu (calculated/prepared) the thing" when I prepared it. The reason for this is that when the revelation came down: "Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the All-Knowing" [Ghafir: 1–2], up to His saying: "To Him is the final return," al-Walid heard it being recited and said: "By Allah, I have heard from him speech that is neither the speech of men nor the speech of jinn. Indeed it has sweetness, and indeed it has radiance upon it. Its upper part is fruitful, and its lower part is abundant. It is surely the one that rises and is not surpassed, and this is not the saying of a human being."

Quraysh said: "al-Walid has inclined (sabā), and all of Quraysh will incline." Al-Walid was called "the fragrant herb of Quraysh" (rayhanat Quraysh). Abu Jahl said: "I will suffice you against him." So he went to him in a state of sorrow, and he said to him: "What is it that I see you sorrowful?" He said: "And why should I not be sorrowful, when these people of Quraysh are gathering money for you, to assist you with it in your old age, and they claim that you have embellished the speech of Muhammad, and that you enter upon the son of Abu Kabshah and the son of Abu Quhafah in order to obtain some of their food?" Al-Walid became angry and grew proud, and he said: "I do not need the crumbs of Muhammad and his companion. You know the measure of my wealth. By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I have no need of that. You only claim that Muhammad is a madman. Have you ever seen him choke (yakhnuq)?" They said: "No, by Allah." He said: "And you claim he is a poet. Have you ever seen him utter poetry?" They said: "No, by Allah." He said: "Then you claim he is a liar. Have you ever tested him with a lie?" They said: "No, by Allah."

He said: "Then you claim he is a soothsayer (kahin). Have you ever seen him practise soothsaying? We have seen the soothsayers' rhymed prose (asjā') and their convulsions (takhalluj) — [[Takhalluj of the madman in his gait: pulling right and left.]] — have you seen him like that?" They said: "No, by Allah." The Prophet ﷺ was called "the Truthful, the Trustworthy" because of how much he spoke the truth. Quraysh said to al-Walid: "Then what is he?" He reflected in himself, then looked, then frowned, and said: "He is nothing but a sorcerer! Have you not seen him separate a man from his wife, his child, and his clients?!" This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he reflected﴾, that is, about the matter of Muhammad and the Qur'an, ﴿and calculated﴾ in himself what he could say about them. ﴿So may he be destroyed (qutila)﴾, that is, cursed. Some of the interpreters said: its meaning is "he was overpowered and defeated, and everything humbled is qutila (slain)." The poet said [[He is Imru' al-Qays.]]:

"Your two eyes did not shed tears except to shoot with your two arrows into the fragments of a slain heart."

Al-Zuhri said: "He was punished," and this is in the mode of supplication. ﴿How he calculated﴾: some people said: "how" is an expression of wonder, as one says to a man whose deed amazes you: "How did you do this?" Like His saying: ﴿Look how they strike similitudes for you﴾ [Al-Isra: 48]. Then ﴿qutila﴾, that is, cursed with a curse after a curse. It was also said: ﴿so he was destroyed﴾ by one kind of punishment, then ﴿destroyed﴾ again by another kind of punishment; ﴿how he calculated﴾, that is, in whatever state he calculated.

(Then he looked) — by what means he might repel and push back the truth.

(Then he frowned) — that is, he knitted his brows at the faces of the believers. That is because when he moved Quraysh to what they had moved to, saying about Muhammad ﷺ that he is a sorcerer, he passed by a group of Muslims, who invited him to Islam, and he frowned in their faces. It was said: he frowned and scowled (basara) at the Prophet ﷺ when he invited him. The word al-'abs (with a light pronunciation) is the verbal noun of ʿabisa, ya'bisu, ʿabsan and ʿubusan: when he knits his brows. Al-'abas is what clings to the tails of camels of their dung and urine. Abu al-Najm said:

"As if in their tails were the shawl (al-shu'ul) of the herd, from the 'abas of summer, the horns of the gazelles."

(And scowled) — that is, his face became contorted and its color changed. This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"We attacked Tamim at dawn at al-Jifar [al-Jifar: a place. It was also said it is a water of the Banu Tamim] with a white, compact host."

And another said [He is Tawbah ibn al-Humayyir. Some copies add after this verse the following marginal note: his saying (bi-shahba'): he meant a white battalion, and from it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And a battalion that I clothed with a battalion, white, brave, whose cloak is feared."

It is said: a battalion mulmalah and mulmumah, i.e., gathered, its parts pressed together. And a stone mulmumah and mulamlamah, i.e., round and hard, as al-Jawhari said.]:

"Her aversion has troubled me, which I have seen, and her turning away from my need, and her scowling."

It was also said: the appearance of frowning on the face comes after the conversation, while the appearance of bisur on the face comes before the conversation. Some said: basara means he stopped, neither advancing nor retreating. They said: the people of Yemen say likewise when a ship halts and neither comes nor goes: "The ship has basara, and absara," i.e., it stopped; and "we have absarna." The Arabs say: "a basir face, clearly bisur," when it has changed and blackened.

(Then he turned away) — that is, he turned and withdrew, going off to his family. (And he was arrogant) — that is, he magnified himself against believing. It was also said: he turned away from faith and was arrogant when he was called to it.

The word al-'abs (with a light pronunciation) is the verbal noun of ʿabisa, ya'bisu, ʿabsan and ʿubusan: when he knits his brows. Al-'abas is what clings to the tails of camels of their dung and urine. Abu al-Najm said:

"As if in their tails were the shawl (al-shu'ul) of the herd, from the 'abas of summer, the horns of the gazelles."

(And scowled) — that is, his face became contorted and its color changed. This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi, and from it is the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"We attacked Tamim at dawn at al-Jifar [al-Jifar: a place. It was also said it is a water of the Banu Tamim] with a white, compact host."

And another said [He is Tawbah ibn al-Humayyir. Some copies add after this verse the following marginal note: his saying (bi-shahba'): he meant a white battalion, and from it is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And a battalion that I clothed with a battalion, white, brave, whose cloak is feared."

It is said: a battalion mulmalah and mulmumah, i.e., gathered, its parts pressed together. And a stone mulmumah and mulamlamah, i.e., round and hard, as al-Jawhari said.]:

"Her aversion has troubled me, which I have seen, and her turning away from my need, and her scowling."

It was also said: the appearance of frowning on the face comes after the conversation, while the appearance of bisur on the face comes before the conversation. Some said: basara means he stopped, neither advancing nor retreating. They said: the people of Yemen say likewise when a ship halts and neither comes nor goes: "The ship has basara, and absara," i.e., it stopped; and "we have absarna." The Arabs say: "a basir face, clearly bisur," when it has changed and blackened.

(Then he turned away) — that is, he turned and withdrew, going off to his family. (And he was arrogant) — that is, he magnified himself against believing. It was also said: he turned away from faith and was arrogant when he was called to it.

Then He said: ﴿Then he said, "This is nothing but magic imitated (yu'thar)"﴾ — that is, what Muhammad ﷺ has brought is nothing but magic that is transmitted (yu'thiruhu) from another. Sihr (magic) is deception. Its explanation has already preceded in Surat al-Baqarah [see 2/p.43]. Some said: sihr is the manifestation of falsehood in the form of truth. Al-Atharah is the verbal noun of your saying: athartu al-hadith, athiruhu, when you narrate it from someone else; from this comes "a transmitted hadith (hadith ma'thur)," i.e., one that a later generation transmits from an earlier one. Imru' al-Qays said [He means: if this news came to me from the narration of another, I would say a saying that would spread among people and be transmitted from me until the end of time. Al-Naba': what is reported of good and evil. Al-Musnad: the time.]:

"And if the report from another's narration had come to me, and the wound of the tongue is like the wound of the hand,
I would have said of speech what would never cease to be transmitted from me, through the hand of the transmitter."

He means: until the end of time. Al-A'sha said:

"Indeed, what you two disputed about has been made clear to the listener and the transmitter."

And it is narrated: bayyana (with a different reading).

﴿This is nothing but the saying of a human being﴾ — that is, this is nothing but the speech of created beings, by which hearts are deceived as they are deceived by sorcery. Al-Suddi said: they meant that it is from the saying of Sayyar, a slave of the Banu al-Hadrami, who used to sit with the Prophet ﷺ, so they accused him of having learned it from him. It was also said: he meant that he received it from the people of Babel. It was said: from Musaylimah. It was said: from 'Adi al-Hadrami the soothsayer. It was said: he only received it from one who claimed prophethood before him, and he wove upon their pattern. Abu Sa'id al-Darir said: ﴿This is nothing but magic (sihr) imitated (yu'thar)﴾, i.e., it is transmitted (yuwrath)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will cause him to enter Saqar﴾, meaning, I will cause him to enter Saqar so that he may burn in its heat. Saqar is so named from the phrase "saqarat-hu al-shams" (the sun scorched him), when it melts him, blackens him, and burns the skin of his face. It is not declined (لَا يَنْصَرِفُ, lā yanṣarif, diptote) because of definiteness and feminine gender.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the sixth layer of Jahannam.

Abu Hurayah narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: [Musa asked his Lord, saying: O Lord, which of Your servants is the poorest? He said: the owner of Saqar.]

al-Tha'labi mentioned it.

His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ This is hyperbole (مُبَالَغَة, mubalagha) in describing it, meaning: and what will inform you what it is? It is a word of magnification. Then He explained its condition, saying: ﴿It spares nothing and leaves nothing﴾, meaning it leaves for them no bone, no flesh, and no blood except that it burns it. The word is repeated for emphasis.

It was also said: it spares nothing of them, then they are returned to a new creation, so it does not leave off re-burning them in this way forever. Mujahid said: it spares no one in it alive, and leaves no one in it dead; it burns them every time they are renewed. al-Suddi said: it spares them no flesh and leaves them no bone.

﴿Scorching to the human being﴾, meaning altering, from "lāḥahu" when it alters him. The common reading is "lawwāḥatun" with the nominative (بِالرَّفْعِ, raf'), as an adjective (نَعْت, na't) of "Saqar" in His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾. 'Aṭiyya al-'Awfi, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "lawwāḥatan" with the accusative, as a specification (عَلَى الِاخْتِصَاصِ, 'alā al-ikhtiṣāṣ) for the purpose of awe-inspiring intimidation (لِلتَّهْوِيلِ, li-l-tahwīl).

Abu Razin said: it scorches their faces with a blaze that leaves them blacker than the night. Mujahid said the same.

The Arabs say: "lāḥahu al-bard, wal-ḥarr, wal-suqm, wal-ḥuzn" (cold, heat, sickness, and grief have altered him) when it changes him. From this is the poet's saying:

"She says: What has altered you, O traveler?
O daughter of my uncle, the midday heats have altered me."

[al-Hawājir: plural of hājira, meaning the intense heat at the middle of the day.]

Another said:

"Hind marvels that she saw me pale,
she says to something the simooms have scorched."

[al-Samā'im: plural of samūm, meaning the hot wind.]

Ru'ba ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

"The journey altered him after plumpness and fullness,
like your scorching of the lean horse that is starved for the race."

[The journey altered and emaciated him. Al-badan: fatness and firmness of flesh. Al-sanaq: satiety to the point of being like a surfeit. The ḍāmir: the horse. Yuṭwā: is made hungry for the sake of racing.]

"She gave me a draught of water with a lawḥ,
may God water her with the drizzling, morning clouds."

He means by al-lawḥ the intensity of thirst. "Iltāḥa" means he became thirsty. Al-rihām: plural of rahma (with a kasra), which is a light rain; "arhamati al-saḥāba" means the cloud brought light rain.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verses 30–31:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾. That is, over Saqar are nineteen angels who cast its inhabitants into it. Then it was said: over the whole of the Fire are nineteen angels who are its guardians (khazanah), Malik and eighteen other angels. It is possible that the nineteen are chiefs (naqib, leaders), and it is possible that they are nineteen angels specifically. Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold this view.

Al-Tha'labi said: This is not to be denied. If one angel takes the souls of all creatures, it is more fitting that nineteen should be over the punishment of some creatures.

Ibn Jurayj said: The Prophet (ﷺ) described the guardians of Hell, saying: [Their eyes are like lightning, their mouths are like the horns (of cattle), they drag their hair. Each one of them has the strength of both humans and jinn together. One of them drives a nation, with a mountain upon his neck, and throws them into the Fire, and throws the mountain on top of them.]

I say: Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned, saying: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from al-Azraq ibn Qays, from a man of the Banu Tamim, who said: We were with Abu al-Awwam, and he recited this verse: ﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is? It leaves nothing and spares nothing. It scorches the human being. Over it are nineteen.﴾ Then he said: What is "nineteen"? Nineteen thousand angels, or nineteen angels? I said: No, rather nineteen angels. He said: And how do you know that? I said: Because of the saying of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And We have not made their number but a trial for those who disbelieve﴾. He said: You are right. They are nineteen angels, and in the hand of each of them is a mirzabah [the mirzabah is an iron rod, and the large hammer of the blacksmith, which has two prongs], with which he strikes one blow, and sends with it into the Fire seventy thousand.

From Amr ibn Dinar: Each one of them pushes with a single push into Hell more than (the tribes of) Rabi'ah and Mudar.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Jabir ibn Abd Allah, who said: Some Jews said to some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of Hell? They said: We do not know, until we ask our Prophet. A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Muhammad, your companions were defeated today! He said: (And how were they defeated?) He said: The Jews asked them: Does your Prophet know the number of the guardians of Hell? He said: (And what did they say?) He said: They said: We do not know, until we ask our Prophet. He said: (Has a people been defeated when they were asked about what they do not know, and said: We do not know, until we ask our Prophet? Rather, they (the Jews) asked their prophet: Show us Allah openly! Bring me the enemies of Allah! I will ask them about the clay of Paradise, which is the fine white flour (darmak).) When they came, they said: O Abu al-Qasim, how many are the guardians of Hell? He said: (Thus and thus), once ten and once nine. They said: Yes. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: (What is the clay of Paradise?) He said: They were silent for a moment, then said: Is it bread, O Abu al-Qasim? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (Bread is made from darmak).

Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi) said: This is a gharib (rare) hadith, which we only know through this route, from the hadith of Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Jabir.

Ibn Wahb mentioned, saying: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd narrated to us, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about the guardians of Hell: [The distance between the shoulders of one of them is like the distance between the east and the west.]

Ibn Abbas said: The distance between the shoulders of one of them is a year's journey, and the strength of one of them is that he strikes with the maqma' (a spiked iron club), and with that one blow he pushes seventy thousand people into the depths of Hell.

I say: The correct view, if Allah wills, is that these nineteen are the chiefs and leaders, while as for their totality, expression falls short of describing them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾. It is established in the Sahih, from Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (On that day Hell will be brought, having seventy thousand reins, with each rein seventy thousand angels dragging it.)

Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: When this was revealed, ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾, Abu Jahl said to the Quraysh: May your mothers be bereaved! I hear that the son of Abu Kabshah tells you that the guardians of Hell are nineteen, while you are the multitude (al-duhm, that is, the numbers) and the brave! Each ten of you would be unable to overcome one of them! Al-Suddi said: Then Abu al-Aswad ibn Kalda al-Jumahi said: Do not let the nineteen frighten you. I will push back ten of the angels with my right shoulder, and nine with my left shoulder, and then you will pass into Paradise. He said this mockingly. In another narration: al-Harith ibn Kalada said: I will suffice you against seventeen, and you suffice me against two. It was also said: Abu Jahl said: Would not each hundred of you be unable to overcome one of them, then you will come out of the Fire? Then the saying of Allah the Exalted was revealed: ﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire but angels﴾, that is, We did not make them men, so that you might contend with them in strength. It was also said: He made them angels because they are of a different kind from the punished among the jinn and humans, so mercy and tenderness do not affect them as they would affect their own kind, and they do not find rest in them; and because they are the most upright of Allah's creation in the right of Allah and in anger for Him, so their leniency is not to be trusted; and because they are the mightiest of Allah's creation in might and the strongest in striking.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas through more than one route, that he said: a misguidance for those who disbelieve, meaning Abu Jahl and his kind. It was also said: a punishment, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The day they will be tried over the Fire. "Taste your trial!"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 14], that is, We made that the cause of their disbelief and the cause of the punishment.

There are seven readings (qira'at) of "nineteen" [the sources contain only six readings, and perhaps the seventh is the reading of Sulayman ibn Qatah: "tis'at a'shur", with the t pronounced with damma, the hamza fathah, the ayn sukun, the shin damma and the ra' kasra. Al-Samin criticized these readings, saying: In this word there are anomalous readings and justifications that accompany them.]: the common reading is tis'ata 'ashara. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Talhah ibn Sulayman read "tis'ata 'shar" with the ayn sukun. From Ibn Abbas: "tis'atu 'ashara" with a damma on the ha'. From Anas ibn Malik: "tis'atu wa'ashar". From him also: "tis'atu wa'ashr". From him also: "tis'atu a'shur", mentioned by al-Mahdawi, who said: Whoever reads "tis'ata 'shar" makes the ayn sukun to avoid successive vowels. Whoever reads "tis'atu wa'ashar" brings it in its original form before the compound, and conjoins 'ashr to tis'a, drops the tanwin for frequency of use, and makes the ra' of 'ashar sukun with the intention of pausing on it. Whoever reads "tis'atu 'ashrin" it is as if it were a kind of contraction (tadakhul), as though he intended the conjunction and left off the compounding, so he raised the feminine ha' and then returned to the construction and made it sukun. Al-Zamakhshari said: It was also read "tis'atu a'shur", the plural of 'ashir, like yamin and aymun.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So that those who were given the Book may be certain﴾, that is, so that those who were given the Torah and the Gospel may be certain that the number of the guardians of Hell agrees with what is in their possession. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and others. Then it is possible that he means those among them who believed, such as Abd Allah ibn Salam. And it is possible that he means all of them.

﴿And that those who believe may increase in faith﴾ through this, because whenever they affirm what is in the Book of Allah they believe, and then they increase in faith by affirming the number of the guardians of Hell. ﴿And that those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾, that is, that those who were given the Book (that is, the Jews and Christians) and the believers (that is, the affirmers among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ)) may not doubt that the number of the guardians of Hell is nineteen.

﴿And that those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, that is, in whose breasts is doubt and hypocrisy, from the hypocrites of the people of Madinah, who emerged in the future time after the Hijrah; hypocrisy did not exist in Makkah, but it emerged in Madinah. It was also said: The meaning is: and that the hypocrites who would emerge in the future time after the Hijrah may say, ﴿and the disbelievers﴾, that is, the Jews and Christians, ﴿"What did Allah intend by this as a parable?"﴾, meaning by the number of the guardians of Hell. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: The surah is Makkan, and there was no hypocrisy in Makkah, so the disease in this verse is disagreement, and "the disbelievers" are the polytheists of the Arabs. According to the first view, most of the exegetes hold. It is permissible that by "disease" is meant doubt and uncertainty, because most of the people of Makkah were doubtful, and some of them were certain of falsehood. The saying of Allah the Exalted, reporting about them: ﴿"What did Allah intend?"﴾, that is, what did He intend by this number which he mentioned as a hadith, that is, what is this from the speech? Al-Layth said: The parable (mathal) is the saying, and from it: ﴿the likeness of the Garden which the righteous are promised﴾, that is, its account and the report about it. ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like Allah's leading astray of Abu Jahl and his companions who denied the guardians of Hell, ﴿Allah leads astray whom He wills﴾, that is, He humiliates and blinds whom He wills, ﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, that is, He guides whom He wills, like the guidance of the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: Thus Allah leads astray from the Garden whom He wills, and guides to it whom He wills.

﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾, that is, none knows the number of your Lord's angels whom He created to punish the people of the Fire, except Him, that is, except Allah, may His praise be exalted. This is an answer to Abu Jahl when he said: Does Muhammad have no hosts except nineteen! It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) was dividing the spoils of Hunayn, when Jibril came and sat beside him. Then an angel came and said: Your Lord commands you to do such and such. The Prophet (ﷺ) feared that it might be a devil, so he said: (O Jibril, do you know him?) He said: He is an angel, and I do not know all the angels of your Lord.

Al-Awza'i said: Musa said: "O Lord, who is in the heaven?" He said: "My angels." He said: "How many are they, O Lord?" He said: "Twelve tribes." He said: "How many is each tribe?" He said: "The number of the dust." Al-Tha'labi mentioned both of these.

In al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet (ﷺ): (The heaven creaks (atta), and it has a right to creak; there is not a place of four fingers in it but an angel is placing his forehead, prostrating to Allah.)

[Al-atit: the sound of the saddle-pad (ikaf) of a camel. The creaking of camels is their sounds and their moaning. That is, the great number of angels in it has weighed it down until it creaks. This is a figure of speech indicating the great number of angels, even if there is no actual creaking. (Al-Nihayah).]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And it is not but a reminder to humanity﴾. It means the proofs, the arguments and the Qur'an. It was also said: ﴿And it is not﴾, that is, this Fire which is Saqar, ﴿but a reminder﴾, that is, an admonition, ﴿to humanity﴾, that is, to creation. It was also said: the fire of this world is a reminder of the fire of the Hereafter. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was also said: That is, this number is only a reminder to humanity, so that they may remember and know the perfection of Allah's power, and that He does not need helpers or supporters. Accordingly, the pronoun in the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And it is not﴾, refers to the hosts, because it is the nearest thing mentioned.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verses 32–48 (part 1 of 2)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, by the moon﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Kalla" is a particle attached to the oath (qasam, "oath"), and the sense is "ay wa-l-qamar" (indeed, by the moon). It was also said that the meaning is "haqqan wa-l-qamar" (truly, by the moon), so it is not to be stopped on "kalla" under either of these readings. Al-Tabari permitted stopping on "kalla" and took it as a rejection of those who claimed they could withstand the guardians of Hell. That is, the matter is not as the one who claims he can resist the guardians of the Fire says. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swore by the moon and by what follows it, saying: ﴿And by the night when it turns back﴾, meaning when it withdraws (wallā), and likewise "dabara."

Nafi', Hamza and Hafs read ﴿idh adbara﴾. The rest read ﴿idha adbara﴾ with an alif, and "dabara" without an alif. Both are dialectal forms with the same meaning: one says "dabara" and "adbara," just as "qabila al-layl" and "aqbala." They have also said: "amsi al-dabir wa-l-mudbir" (yesterday). Sakhr ibn 'Amr ibn al-Sharid al-Sulami said:

*"We have slain you in plenty and in multitude, and we have left Murrah like yesterday that has passed."*

It is also transmitted as "al-mudbir." This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. Some lexicographers said: "dabara al-layl" means it has passed, and "adbara" means it has begun to withdraw. Mujahid said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the words of Allah, ﴿And by the night when it dabara﴾, and he was silent until it had dabara, then he said: "O Mujahid, this is the time when the night has dabara."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿wa-l-layli idh adbara﴾ with two alifs, and so it is in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy with two alifs. Qutrub said: whoever reads "dabara" means "aqbala" (came forward), from the Arab saying "dabara fulan" when he came from behind me. Abu 'Amr said: this is the dialect of Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas said in one narration: the correct reading is "adbara," for only the back of a camel is "dubr." Abu 'Ubayd chose "idha adbara," saying: it agrees more with the letters that follow it. Do you not see that Allah says ﴿wa-l-subhi idha asfar﴾ (and by the dawn when it brightens)? How could one of them be "idh" and the other "idha," when the Qur'an contains no oath followed by "idh," but only by "idha"? The meaning of "asfara" is "ḍā'a" (shone). The common reading is "asfara" with an alif, and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "safara." Both are dialectal forms. One says "safara wajhu fulan" and "asfara," meaning it shone. A hadith says: "Asfiru bi-l-fajr, fa-innahu a'zam li-l-ajr" (Perform the dawn prayer while it is still bright, for it is greater in reward). That is, pray the dawn prayer while the light is clear. It is said: prolong it until the brightening (al-isfar), and al-isfar is illumination. "Asfara wajhuhu husnan" means his face shone with beauty. "Safarati al-mar'ah" means the woman uncovered her face, and she is "sāfir." It is also possible that it comes from "safara al-zalam," meaning he swept away the darkness, just as the house is "yusfar," that is, swept. From this comes "al-safir," for what has fallen from the leaves of trees and been shed; it is said it is called "safir" because the wind sweeps it away, that is, sweeps it clean. "Al-misfara" is the broom.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (al-kubar)﴾. This is the answer to the oath: that is, this Fire is indeed one of the greatest, that is, one of the great calamities. In the tafsir of Muqatil, "al-kubar" is a name of the Fire. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is indeed one of the greatest, that is, a grave sin among the major sins. It was also said: the Hour's coming is indeed one of the greatest. "Al-kubar" means the great punishments. The rajaz poet said:

*"O son of al-Mu'alla, one of the greatest has descended, the calamity of time and the deaf one of changes."*

The singular of "al-kubar" is "kubra," like "al-sughra" and "al-sughar," and "al-'uzma" and "al-'uzam." The common reading is ﴿la-ihdā al-kubar﴾, and "ihdā" is a noun formed from the start as feminine. It is not built on the masculine, like "'uqbā" and "ukhrā." Its alif is an alif of cutting (hamzat al-qat'), which is not dropped in connected speech. Jarir ibn Hazim narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿innaha la-hda al-kubar﴾ with the hamza omitted.

Allah says: ﴿A warning to mankind﴾. It means the Fire: that this described Fire is a warning to mankind. "Nadhiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "innaha," as al-Zajjaj said. It is masculine because its meaning is the punishment (al-'adhab), or it intends "dhāt indhār" (a thing of warning) in the sense of attribution, like the Arabs' saying "imra'ah ṭāliq" and "ṭāhir." Al-Khalil said: "al-nadhir" is a verbal noun like "al-nakir," and for this reason it is applied to the feminine. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, mankind has not been warned with anything more calamitous than it. It was also said: the intended "nadhir" is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: "Stand up as a warner to mankind," that is, frightening them. Then "nadhiran" is a circumstantial accusative from "qum" at the beginning of the surah, when He said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:2]. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Zayd, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but al-Farra' rejected it. Ibn al-Anbari said: some exegetes said its meaning is "O you who are wrapped, arise as a warner to mankind." This is ugly, because the speech has been lengthened between them.

It was also said that it is an attribute of Allah, Exalted. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 32–48 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. This is evidence for the validity of intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because a people from among the People of Monotheism (ahl al-tawhid) were punished for their sins, then intercession was made for them, so Allah had mercy on them through their monotheism and the intercession, and they were brought out of the Fire. And there is no intercessor for the disbelievers who would intercede on their behalf.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) will intercede fourth of four: Jibril, then Ibrahim, then Musa or Isa [[In manuscripts H and L: "and Isa".]], then your Prophet (ﷺ), then the angels, then the prophets, then the truthful ones (al-siddiqun), then the martyrs. And there will remain a people in Jahannam, and it will be said to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor..." up to His saying: ﴿so the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: These are the ones who will remain in Jahannam. We have mentioned its chain of transmission (isnad) in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

This is evidence for the validity of intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because a people from among the People of Monotheism (ahl al-tawhid) were punished for their sins, then intercession was made for them, so Allah had mercy on them through their monotheism and the intercession, and they were brought out of the Fire. And there is no intercessor for the disbelievers who would intercede on their behalf.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) will intercede fourth of four: Jibril, then Ibrahim, then Musa or Isa [[In manuscripts H and L: "and Isa".]], then your Prophet (ﷺ), then the angels, then the prophets, then the truthful ones (al-siddiqun), then the martyrs. And there will remain a people in Jahannam, and it will be said to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor..." up to His saying: ﴿so the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: These are the ones who will remain in Jahannam. We have mentioned its chain of transmission (isnad) in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verses 32–48 (part 1 of 2)**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Nay, by the moon﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Kalla" is a particle attached to the oath (qasam, "oath"), and the sense is "ay wa-l-qamar" (indeed, by the moon). It was also said that the meaning is "haqqan wa-l-qamar" (truly, by the moon), so it is not to be stopped on "kalla" under either of these readings. Al-Tabari permitted stopping on "kalla" and took it as a rejection of those who claimed they could withstand the guardians of Hell. That is, the matter is not as the one who claims he can resist the guardians of the Fire says. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swore by the moon and by what follows it, saying: ﴿And by the night when it turns back﴾, meaning when it withdraws (wallā), and likewise "dabara."

Nafi', Hamza and Hafs read ﴿idh adbara﴾. The rest read ﴿idha adbara﴾ with an alif, and "dabara" without an alif. Both are dialectal forms with the same meaning: one says "dabara" and "adbara," just as "qabila al-layl" and "aqbala." They have also said: "amsi al-dabir wa-l-mudbir" (yesterday). Sakhr ibn 'Amr ibn al-Sharid al-Sulami said:

*"We have slain you in plenty and in multitude, and we have left Murrah like yesterday that has passed."*

It is also transmitted as "al-mudbir." This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Akhfash. Some lexicographers said: "dabara al-layl" means it has passed, and "adbara" means it has begun to withdraw. Mujahid said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the words of Allah, ﴿And by the night when it dabara﴾, and he was silent until it had dabara, then he said: "O Mujahid, this is the time when the night has dabara."

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa read ﴿wa-l-layli idh adbara﴾ with two alifs, and so it is in the codices of Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy with two alifs. Qutrub said: whoever reads "dabara" means "aqbala" (came forward), from the Arab saying "dabara fulan" when he came from behind me. Abu 'Amr said: this is the dialect of Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas said in one narration: the correct reading is "adbara," for only the back of a camel is "dubr." Abu 'Ubayd chose "idha adbara," saying: it agrees more with the letters that follow it. Do you not see that Allah says ﴿wa-l-subhi idha asfar﴾ (and by the dawn when it brightens)? How could one of them be "idh" and the other "idha," when the Qur'an contains no oath followed by "idh," but only by "idha"? The meaning of "asfara" is "ḍā'a" (shone). The common reading is "asfara" with an alif, and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "safara." Both are dialectal forms. One says "safara wajhu fulan" and "asfara," meaning it shone. A hadith says: "Asfiru bi-l-fajr, fa-innahu a'zam li-l-ajr" (Perform the dawn prayer while it is still bright, for it is greater in reward). That is, pray the dawn prayer while the light is clear. It is said: prolong it until the brightening (al-isfar), and al-isfar is illumination. "Asfara wajhuhu husnan" means his face shone with beauty. "Safarati al-mar'ah" means the woman uncovered her face, and she is "sāfir." It is also possible that it comes from "safara al-zalam," meaning he swept away the darkness, just as the house is "yusfar," that is, swept. From this comes "al-safir," for what has fallen from the leaves of trees and been shed; it is said it is called "safir" because the wind sweeps it away, that is, sweeps it clean. "Al-misfara" is the broom.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (al-kubar)﴾. This is the answer to the oath: that is, this Fire is indeed one of the greatest, that is, one of the great calamities. In the tafsir of Muqatil, "al-kubar" is a name of the Fire. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is indeed one of the greatest, that is, a grave sin among the major sins. It was also said: the Hour's coming is indeed one of the greatest. "Al-kubar" means the great punishments. The rajaz poet said:

*"O son of al-Mu'alla, one of the greatest has descended, the calamity of time and the deaf one of changes."*

The singular of "al-kubar" is "kubra," like "al-sughra" and "al-sughar," and "al-'uzma" and "al-'uzam." The common reading is ﴿la-ihdā al-kubar﴾, and "ihdā" is a noun formed from the start as feminine. It is not built on the masculine, like "'uqbā" and "ukhrā." Its alif is an alif of cutting (hamzat al-qat'), which is not dropped in connected speech. Jarir ibn Hazim narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿innaha la-hda al-kubar﴾ with the hamza omitted.

Allah says: ﴿A warning to mankind﴾. It means the Fire: that this described Fire is a warning to mankind. "Nadhiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "innaha," as al-Zajjaj said. It is masculine because its meaning is the punishment (al-'adhab), or it intends "dhāt indhār" (a thing of warning) in the sense of attribution, like the Arabs' saying "imra'ah ṭāliq" and "ṭāhir." Al-Khalil said: "al-nadhir" is a verbal noun like "al-nakir," and for this reason it is applied to the feminine. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, mankind has not been warned with anything more calamitous than it. It was also said: the intended "nadhir" is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: "Stand up as a warner to mankind," that is, frightening them. Then "nadhiran" is a circumstantial accusative from "qum" at the beginning of the surah, when He said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:2]. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Zayd, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but al-Farra' rejected it. Ibn al-Anbari said: some exegetes said its meaning is "O you who are wrapped, arise as a warner to mankind." This is ugly, because the speech has been lengthened between them.

It was also said that it is an attribute of Allah, Exalted. Abu Mu'awiya al-Darir narrated: Isma'il ibn Sami' narrated to us from Abu Razin concerning "nadhiran li-l-bashar," that he said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I am a warner to you from it, so beware of it." On this view, "nadhiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative, meaning: "We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, a warning to those mankind." It was also said that it is a circumstantial accusative from "huwa" in the words of Allah: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]. It was also said that it is in the place of a verbal noun, as if He said "indhār li-l-bashar" (a warning to mankind). Al-Farra' said: "al-nadhir" may mean "al-indhār" (warning), that is, "andhir indhāran," as in the words of Allah: ﴿So how was My warning?﴾ [al-Mulk 67:18], that is, "My warning." On this view it refers back to the beginning of the surah, meaning: "Arise and warn," that is, a warning. It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "nadhirun" in the nominative, as an implied "huwa" (it is). It was also said: the Qur'an is a warning to mankind, because of what it contains of promise and threat.

Allah says: ﴿For whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾. The "li-" (for) is connected to "nadhiran," meaning: a warner for whoever among you wills to go forward toward goodness and obedience, or to lag behind toward evil and disobedience. Its parallel is the words of Allah: ﴿And We certainly know those of you who go forward﴾ [al-Hijr 15:24], meaning in goodness, and ﴿And We certainly know those who lag behind﴾ [al-Hijr 15:24], meaning from it. Al-Hasan said: this is a threat and an intimidation, even though it is in the form of a statement, like the words of Allah: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29]. Some exegetes said: the meaning is "for whomever Allah wills to go forward or lag behind," so the will is attached to Allah, Exalted be His praise, and "going forward" is faith, while "lagging behind" is disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: this is a threat and an announcement that whoever goes forward to obedience and faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) will be rewarded with a reward that does not end, and whoever lags behind from obedience and denies Muhammad (ﷺ) will be punished with a punishment that does not end. Al-Suddi said: for whoever among you wills to go forward to the Fire mentioned before, or lag behind from it to Paradise.

Allah says: ﴿Every soul, for what it has earned, is held in pledge﴾. That is, it is pledged (murtahanah) by its earning, taken to account for its deed: either He frees it, or He destroys it. The word "rahīnah" here is not the feminine of "rahīn" in the words of Allah: ﴿Every man, for what he has earned, is held in pledge﴾ [al-Tur 52:21], for the feminine of the soul (al-nafs). For if the adjective were intended, it would be said "rahīn," because "fa'īl" in the sense of "maf'ūl" is the same for masculine and feminine. Rather, it is a noun in the sense of "al-rahn" (pledge), like "al-shatīmah" in the sense of "al-shatm" (insult), as if it were said: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From it is the verse of the Hamasah:

*"Is it far that he who is at Na'f Kuwaykib is a pledge of a grave of earth and gravel?"* [[Al-Na'f: the raised place in an obstacle. The verse is from the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd al-'Udhri, whose brother was killed and to whom blood-money was offered, but he refused to take it and took vengeance for his brother.]]

It is as if he said "rahnu ramsin" (a pledge of a grave). The meaning is: every soul is a pledge with Allah for its earning, not released, ﴿except the companions of the right hand﴾, for they are not held in pledge for their sins. The identity of these people is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the angels. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: they are the children of the Muslims, who have not earned, so they are not held in pledge for their earning. Al-Dahhak said: they are those for whom the best reward has preceded from Allah. Similar was narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: every soul is accountable for its deed, except the companions of the right hand, who are the people of Paradise, for they are not called to account. Muqatil also said likewise: they are the people of Paradise who were on the right of Adam on the Day of the Covenant, when Allah said to them: "These are in Paradise, and I do not mind." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims who are not held in pledge, because they fulfilled what was upon them. From Abu Dhabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: they are the Muslims. It was also said: they are the companions of truth and the people of faith. It was also said: they are those who are given their books in their right hands. Abu Ja'far al-Baqir said: we and our Shi'ah are the companions of the right hand, and everyone who hates us, the People of the House, they are the ones held in pledge. Al-Hakam said: they are those whom Allah chose for His service, so they did not enter into the pledge, for they are the servants of Allah and His elect, and their earning did not harm them. Al-Qasim said: every soul is taken to account for its earning, good or evil, except whoever relies on grace and mercy rather than earning and service. Whoever relies on earning is pledged, and whoever relies on grace is not taken to account for it.

Allah says: ﴿In gardens﴾, that is, in orchards. ﴿They will ask one another﴾, that is, they will ask ﴿about the criminals﴾, that is, the polytheists: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾, that is, what has made you enter into Saqar. It is like your saying "salaktu al-khayṭ fi kadhā" (I threaded the thread into such-and-such), meaning I made it enter. Al-Kalbi said: a man of the people of Paradise asks a man of the people of the Fire by his name, and says to him: "O so-and-so." In the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar?" It is also narrated from him that he said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab read "O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar," and this is a reading by way of interpretation, not that it is Qur'an, as whoever attacks the Qur'an claims. This was said by Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: the believers ask the angels about their relatives, and the angels ask the polytheists, and they say to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" Al-Farra' said: in this there is what strengthens the view that the companions of the right hand are the children, for they do not know sins. ﴿They will say﴾, meaning the people of the Fire: ﴿We were not of those who prayed﴾, that is, the believers who used to pray.

﴿And we did not feed the poor﴾, that is, we did not give charity.

﴿And we used to plunge with the plungers﴾, that is, we used to mix with the people of falsehood in their falsehood. Ibn Zayd said: we plunged with the plungers concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is their saying, may Allah curse them: "a soothsayer, a madman, a poet, a sorcerer."

Al-Suddi said: that is, we used to deny with the deniers. Qatada said: whenever a deviator went astray, we went astray with him. It was also said that the meaning is: we were followers and not leaders.

﴿And we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾, that is, we did not believe in the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Recompense and Judgment.

Allah says: ﴿Until there came to us the certainty﴾, that is, death came to us and descended upon us. From this is the words of Allah: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr 15:99].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 32–48 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. This is evidence for the validity of intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because a people from among the People of Monotheism (ahl al-tawhid) were punished for their sins, then intercession was made for them, so Allah had mercy on them through their monotheism and the intercession, and they were brought out of the Fire. And there is no intercessor for the disbelievers who would intercede on their behalf.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) will intercede fourth of four: Jibril, then Ibrahim, then Musa or Isa [[In manuscripts H and L: "and Isa".]], then your Prophet (ﷺ), then the angels, then the prophets, then the truthful ones (al-siddiqun), then the martyrs. And there will remain a people in Jahannam, and it will be said to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor..." up to His saying: ﴿so the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: These are the ones who will remain in Jahannam. We have mentioned its chain of transmission (isnad) in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

"Safarati al-mar'ah" means the woman uncovered her face, and she is "sāfir." It is also possible that it comes from "safara al-zalam," meaning he swept away the darkness, just as the house is "yusfar," that is, swept. From this comes "al-safir," for what has fallen from the leaves of trees and been shed; it is said it is called "safir" because the wind sweeps it away, that is, sweeps it clean. "Al-misfara" is the broom.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, it is one of the greatest (al-kubar)﴾. This is the answer to the oath: that is, this Fire is indeed one of the greatest, that is, one of the great calamities. In the tafsir of Muqatil, "al-kubar" is a name of the Fire. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ) is indeed one of the greatest, that is, a grave sin among the major sins. It was also said: the Hour's coming is indeed one of the greatest. "Al-kubar" means the great punishments. The rajaz poet said:

*"O son of al-Mu'alla, one of the greatest has descended, the calamity of time and the deaf one of changes."*

The singular of "al-kubar" is "kubra," like "al-sughra" and "al-sughar," and "al-'uzma" and "al-'uzam." The common reading is ﴿la-ihdā al-kubar﴾, and "ihdā" is a noun formed from the start as feminine. It is not built on the masculine, like "'uqbā" and "ukhrā." Its alif is an alif of cutting (hamzat al-qat'), which is not dropped in connected speech. Jarir ibn Hazim narrated from Ibn Kathir: ﴿innaha la-hda al-kubar﴾ with the hamza omitted.

Allah says: ﴿A warning to mankind﴾. It means the Fire: that this described Fire is a warning to mankind. "Nadhiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "innaha," as al-Zajjaj said. It is masculine because its meaning is the punishment (al-'adhab), or it intends "dhāt indhār" (a thing of warning) in the sense of attribution, like the Arabs' saying "imra'ah ṭāliq" and "ṭāhir." Al-Khalil said: "al-nadhir" is a verbal noun like "al-nakir," and for this reason it is applied to the feminine. Al-Hasan said: By Allah, mankind has not been warned with anything more calamitous than it. It was also said: the intended "nadhir" is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: "Stand up as a warner to mankind," that is, frightening them. Then "nadhiran" is a circumstantial accusative from "qum" at the beginning of the surah, when He said: ﴿Arise and warn﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:2]. This was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Zayd, and it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but al-Farra' rejected it. Ibn al-Anbari said: some exegetes said its meaning is "O you who are wrapped, arise as a warner to mankind." This is ugly, because the speech has been lengthened between them.

It was also said that it is an attribute of Allah, Exalted. Abu Mu'awiya al-Darir narrated: Isma'il ibn Sami' narrated to us from Abu Razin concerning "nadhiran li-l-bashar," that he said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I am a warner to you from it, so beware of it." On this view, "nadhiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative, meaning: "We have not made the companions of the Fire except angels, a warning to those mankind." It was also said that it is a circumstantial accusative from "huwa" in the words of Allah: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:31]. It was also said that it is in the place of a verbal noun, as if He said "indhār li-l-bashar" (a warning to mankind). Al-Farra' said: "al-nadhir" may mean "al-indhār" (warning), that is, "andhir indhāran," as in the words of Allah: ﴿So how was My warning?﴾ [al-Mulk 67:18], that is, "My warning." On this view it refers back to the beginning of the surah, meaning: "Arise and warn," that is, a warning. It was also said that it is accusative by an implied verb. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "nadhirun" in the nominative, as an implied "huwa" (it is). It was also said: the Qur'an is a warning to mankind, because of what it contains of promise and threat.

Allah says: ﴿For whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾. The "li-" (for) is connected to "nadhiran," meaning: a warner for whoever among you wills to go forward toward goodness and obedience, or to lag behind toward evil and disobedience. Its parallel is the words of Allah: ﴿And We certainly know those of you who go forward﴾ [al-Hijr 15:24], meaning in goodness, and ﴿And We certainly know those who lag behind﴾ [al-Hijr 15:24], meaning from it. Al-Hasan said: this is a threat and an intimidation, even though it is in the form of a statement, like the words of Allah: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf 18:29]. Some exegetes said: the meaning is "for whomever Allah wills to go forward or lag behind," so the will is attached to Allah, Exalted be His praise, and "going forward" is faith, while "lagging behind" is disbelief. Ibn 'Abbas used to say: this is a threat and an announcement that whoever goes forward to obedience and faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) will be rewarded with a reward that does not end, and whoever lags behind from obedience and denies Muhammad (ﷺ) will be punished with a punishment that does not end. Al-Suddi said: for whoever among you wills to go forward to the Fire mentioned before, or lag behind from it to Paradise.

Allah says: ﴿Every soul, for what it has earned, is held in pledge﴾. That is, it is pledged (murtahanah) by its earning, taken to account for its deed: either He frees it, or He destroys it. The word "rahīnah" here is not the feminine of "rahīn" in the words of Allah: ﴿Every man, for what he has earned, is held in pledge﴾ [al-Tur 52:21], for the feminine of the soul (al-nafs). For if the adjective were intended, it would be said "rahīn," because "fa'īl" in the sense of "maf'ūl" is the same for masculine and feminine. Rather, it is a noun in the sense of "al-rahn" (pledge), like "al-shatīmah" in the sense of "al-shatm" (insult), as if it were said: every soul, for what it has earned, is a pledge. From it is the verse of the Hamasah:

*"Is it far that he who is at Na'f Kuwaykib is a pledge of a grave of earth and gravel?"* [[Al-Na'f: the raised place in an obstacle. The verse is from the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd al-'Udhri, whose brother was killed and to whom blood-money was offered, but he refused to take it and took vengeance for his brother.]]

It is as if he said "rahnu ramsin" (a pledge of a grave). The meaning is: every soul is a pledge with Allah for its earning, not released, ﴿except the companions of the right hand﴾, for they are not held in pledge for their sins. The identity of these people is disputed. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the angels. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: they are the children of the Muslims, who have not earned, so they are not held in pledge for their earning. Al-Dahhak said: they are those for whom the best reward has preceded from Allah. Similar was narrated from Ibn Juraij, who said: every soul is accountable for its deed, except the companions of the right hand, who are the people of Paradise, for they are not called to account. Muqatil also said likewise: they are the people of Paradise who were on the right of Adam on the Day of the Covenant, when Allah said to them: "These are in Paradise, and I do not mind." Al-Hasan and Ibn Kaysan said: they are the sincere Muslims who are not held in pledge, because they fulfilled what was upon them. From Abu Dhabyan, from Ibn 'Abbas, he said: they are the Muslims. It was also said: they are the companions of truth and the people of faith. It was also said: they are those who are given their books in their right hands. Abu Ja'far al-Baqir said: we and our Shi'ah are the companions of the right hand, and everyone who hates us, the People of the House, they are the ones held in pledge. Al-Hakam said: they are those whom Allah chose for His service, so they did not enter into the pledge, for they are the servants of Allah and His elect, and their earning did not harm them. Al-Qasim said: every soul is taken to account for its earning, good or evil, except whoever relies on grace and mercy rather than earning and service. Whoever relies on earning is pledged, and whoever relies on grace is not taken to account for it.

Allah says: ﴿In gardens﴾, that is, in orchards. ﴿They will ask one another﴾, that is, they will ask ﴿about the criminals﴾, that is, the polytheists: ﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾, that is, what has made you enter into Saqar. It is like your saying "salaktu al-khayṭ fi kadhā" (I threaded the thread into such-and-such), meaning I made it enter. Al-Kalbi said: a man of the people of Paradise asks a man of the people of the Fire by his name, and says to him: "O so-and-so." In the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: "O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar?" It is also narrated from him that he said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab read "O so-and-so, what has brought you into Saqar," and this is a reading by way of interpretation, not that it is Qur'an, as whoever attacks the Qur'an claims. This was said by Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari. It was also said: the believers ask the angels about their relatives, and the angels ask the polytheists, and they say to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" Al-Farra' said: in this there is what strengthens the view that the companions of the right hand are the children, for they do not know sins. ﴿They will say﴾, meaning the people of the Fire: ﴿We were not of those who prayed﴾, that is, the believers who used to pray.

﴿And we did not feed the poor﴾, that is, we did not give charity.

﴿And we used to plunge with the plungers﴾, that is, we used to mix with the people of falsehood in their falsehood. Ibn Zayd said: we plunged with the plungers concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is their saying, may Allah curse them: "a soothsayer, a madman, a poet, a sorcerer."

Al-Suddi said: that is, we used to deny with the deniers. Qatada said: whenever a deviator went astray, we went astray with him. It was also said that the meaning is: we were followers and not leaders.

﴿And we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾, that is, we did not believe in the Day of Resurrection, the Day of Recompense and Judgment.

Allah says: ﴿Until there came to us the certainty﴾, that is, death came to us and descended upon us. From this is the words of Allah: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr 15:99].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 32–48 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. This is evidence for the validity of intercession (shafa'ah) for the sinners, because a people from among the People of Monotheism (ahl al-tawhid) were punished for their sins, then intercession was made for them, so Allah had mercy on them through their monotheism and the intercession, and they were brought out of the Fire. And there is no intercessor for the disbelievers who would intercede on their behalf.

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Your Prophet (ﷺ) will intercede fourth of four: Jibril, then Ibrahim, then Musa or Isa [[In manuscripts H and L: "and Isa".]], then your Prophet (ﷺ), then the angels, then the prophets, then the truthful ones (al-siddiqun), then the martyrs. And there will remain a people in Jahannam, and it will be said to them: "What has brought you into Saqar?" They will say: "We were not among those who prayed, and we did not feed the poor..." up to His saying: ﴿so the intercession of those who intercede will not benefit them﴾. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud said: These are the ones who will remain in Jahannam. We have mentioned its chain of transmission (isnad) in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 49–53:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder?﴾ That is, what is wrong with the people of Makkah that they turned away and fled from what you have brought?

In the tafsir of Muqatil: turning away from the Qur'an takes two forms. The first is denial and rejection; the second is not acting upon what it contains. The word ﴿turning away﴾ (mu'ridin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the hā' and mīm in lahum, and in the lām there is the meaning of a verb, so the accusative of the state is according to that implied verb meaning. ﴿As if they were﴾ (ka-annahum), that is, as if these disbelievers, in their fleeing from Muhammad (ﷺ), were ﴿frightened donkeys﴾ (ḥumurun mustanfiratun). Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant wild donkeys.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (mustanfiratun) with a fatha on the fa', meaning ﴿startled and terrified﴾ (munaffiratun, madhu'ratun), and this reading was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The rest read it with a kasra, meaning ﴿fleeing﴾ (nafiratun). It is said: nafarat and istanfarat have the same meaning, like 'ajibtu and ista'jabtu, and sakhirtu and istaskhartu. Al-Farra' recited:

Hold your donkey, for it is startled
In pursuit of female donkeys who have gathered at Gharrib [[Gharrib (with a fatha on the first letter and a sukun... a place name and a mountain before al-Sham in the land of Banu Kilab.]]

Allah the Exalted said [[The phrase (Allah the Exalted said) and the word (fled) are missing from manuscripts A and H.]]: ﴿they fled from a lion (qaswarah)﴾, that is, they bolted and fled from ﴿qaswarah﴾, meaning from archers who shoot at them. Some of the lexicographers said: qaswarah means the archer, and its plural is qaswarah. Likewise Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Kaysan said: qaswarah refers to the archers and hunters. This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas, and by Abu [Zabyan [[In the originals it reads (Abu Hayyan), which is an error; the correction is from al-Tha'labi's tafsir (and al-Tahdhib).]]] from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari. It was also said that it is the lion, as stated by Abu Hurayrah and also Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Arafah said: it derives from qasr, meaning subjugation, i.e., it overpowers beasts of prey, and wild donkeys flee from beasts of prey. Abu Jamrah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: I do not know qaswarah to mean lion in the language of any of the Arabs; rather, it is a gathering of men. He said: so qaswarah is a collection of men, and he recited:

O daughter, be good so that you may be chosen by the good man,
Whose maternal relatives are the jinn and the people of the qaswarah.

And from him: ruku' al-nas, that is, their sound and voices. And from him also: ﴿fled from a qaswarah﴾, that is, from the snares of hunters. And from him also: qaswarah in the tongue of the Arabs is the lion, in the tongue of the Abyssinians is the archers, in the tongue of Persia is shir, and in the tongue of the Nabateans is aryа. Ibn al-A'rabi said: qaswarah is the beginning of the night, meaning they fled from the darkness of the night. 'Ikrimah also said this. It was said: it is the first darkness of the night, and the last darkness of the night is not called qaswarah. Zayd ibn Aslam said: it refers to strong men, and everything strong among the Arabs is qaswarah and qaswar. Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

When we raise a cry in our assemblies,
The returning men, the qasawir, come to us.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, each one of them desires to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, to be given books that are opened. This was because Abu Jahl and a group of Quraysh said: "O Muhammad! Bring us books from the Lord of the worlds in which it is written: 'I have sent Muhammad to you.'" A parallel is: ﴿And we will not believe in your ascent until you send down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra' 93]. Ibn 'Abbas said: they used to say, "If Muhammad is truthful, then let there be at the morning of each one of us a scroll in which is his acquittal and his safety from the Fire." Matar al-Warraq said: they wanted to be given without any deed. Al-Kalbi said: the polytheists said, "We have heard that a man from the Children of Israel would find written at his head his sin and its expiation in the morning, so bring us the like of that." Mujahid said: they wanted a book to be sent down to each one of them containing from Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "To so-and-so son of so-and-so." It was also said: the meaning is that one should be mentioned with good remembrance, so the scrolls were used metaphorically in place of remembrance. They also said: if a person's sins are written against him, why do we not see that? ﴿No!﴾ (kalla), that is, that will not happen. It was also said: it means "truly." The first is better, because it is a rejection of their statement. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, that is, I will not give them what they wish, because they do not fear the Hereafter, being deceived by the world.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (suhufan munshharatan) with a sukun on the ḥā' and the nūn. As for the sukun on the ḥā', it is a lightening; as for the nūn, it is irregular. One only says nashshartu al-thawb and the like, and one does not say anshartu. It is possible that he likened the scroll to the dead, as if it were dead when folded, and when it is unfolded it comes to life, so it was formed on the pattern of ansharahu Allah al-mayyit (God brought the dead to life), just as the bringing back of the dead was likened to the spreading of a garment, and it was said nashara Allah al-mayyit; so it is a dialect form for it.

O daughter, be good so that you may be chosen by the good man,
Whose maternal relatives are the jinn and the people of the qaswarah.

And from him: ruku' al-nas, that is, their sound and voices. And from him also: ﴿fled from a qaswarah﴾, that is, from the snares of hunters. And from him also: qaswarah in the tongue of the Arabs is the lion, in the tongue of the Abyssinians is the archers, in the tongue of Persia is shir, and in the tongue of the Nabateans is aryа. Ibn al-A'rabi said: qaswarah is the beginning of the night, meaning they fled from the darkness of the night. 'Ikrimah also said this. It was said: it is the first darkness of the night, and the last darkness of the night is not called qaswarah. Zayd ibn Aslam said: it refers to strong men, and everything strong among the Arabs is qaswarah and qaswar. Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

When we raise a cry in our assemblies,
The returning men, the qasawir, come to us.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, each one of them desires to be given scrolls spread open﴾, that is, to be given books that are opened. This was because Abu Jahl and a group of Quraysh said: "O Muhammad! Bring us books from the Lord of the worlds in which it is written: 'I have sent Muhammad to you.'" A parallel is: ﴿And we will not believe in your ascent until you send down to us a book we can read﴾ [al-Isra' 93]. Ibn 'Abbas said: they used to say, "If Muhammad is truthful, then let there be at the morning of each one of us a scroll in which is his acquittal and his safety from the Fire." Matar al-Warraq said: they wanted to be given without any deed. Al-Kalbi said: the polytheists said, "We have heard that a man from the Children of Israel would find written at his head his sin and its expiation in the morning, so bring us the like of that." Mujahid said: they wanted a book to be sent down to each one of them containing from Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "To so-and-so son of so-and-so." It was also said: the meaning is that one should be mentioned with good remembrance, so the scrolls were used metaphorically in place of remembrance. They also said: if a person's sins are written against him, why do we not see that? ﴿No!﴾ (kalla), that is, that will not happen. It was also said: it means "truly." The first is better, because it is a rejection of their statement. ﴿Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter﴾, that is, I will not give them what they wish, because they do not fear the Hereafter, being deceived by the world.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (suhufan munshharatan) with a sukun on the ḥā' and the nūn. As for the sukun on the ḥā', it is a lightening; as for the nūn, it is irregular. One only says nashshartu al-thawb and the like, and one does not say anshartu. It is possible that he likened the scroll to the dead, as if it were dead when folded, and when it is unfolded it comes to life, so it was formed on the pattern of ansharahu Allah al-mayyit (God brought the dead to life), just as the bringing back of the dead was likened to the spreading of a garment, and it was said nashara Allah al-mayyit; so it is a dialect form for it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 74, verse 49–53:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder?﴾ That is, what is wrong with the people of Makkah that they turned away and fled from what you have brought?

In the tafsir of Muqatil: turning away from the Qur'an takes two forms. The first is denial and rejection; the second is not acting upon what it contains. The word ﴿turning away﴾ (mu'ridin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the hā' and mīm in lahum, and in the lām there is the meaning of a verb, so the accusative of the state is according to that implied verb meaning. ﴿As if they were﴾ (ka-annahum), that is, as if these disbelievers, in their fleeing from Muhammad (ﷺ), were ﴿frightened donkeys﴾ (ḥumurun mustanfiratun). Ibn 'Abbas said: he meant wild donkeys.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read (mustanfiratun) with a fatha on the fa', meaning ﴿startled and terrified﴾ (munaffiratun, madhu'ratun), and this reading was preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim. The rest read it with a kasra, meaning ﴿fleeing﴾ (nafiratun). It is said: nafarat and istanfarat have the same meaning, like 'ajibtu and ista'jabtu, and sakhirtu and istaskhartu. Al-Farra' recited:

Hold your donkey, for it is startled
In pursuit of female donkeys who have gathered at Gharrib [[Gharrib (with a fatha on the first letter and a sukun... a place name and a mountain before al-Sham in the land of Banu Kilab.]]
